questions.title: Writing and Estimating User Stories for a BI Deliverable in Sprint Planning
questions.prompt: Your Scrum team is planning the next sprint. Product wants 'a dashboard showing customer lifetime value by region' as a single backlog item, estimated at 3 story points by a junior analyst who hasn't scoped the data sources yet. As the senior BI person on the team, you suspect this is actually multiple stories hiding inside one, with real uncertainty in the CLV calculation logic and an unvalidated data source. How do you handle this in backlog grooming?
questions.modelAnswer:
A strong answer uses backlog grooming to decompose the vague item into independently valuable, estimable stories rather than accepting or silently re-estimating a single large story. The candidate should describe splitting it along natural seams: a story to validate and document the CLV calculation logic with the business stakeholder, a story to confirm and connect the required data sources, a story to build the underlying semantic model/measures, and a story for the dashboard visualization itself — each with its own acceptance criteria.

The candidate should explain why the junior analyst's 3-point estimate was likely too low without undermining them in front of the team: the estimate was made before the unknowns (calculation logic, data source validation) were surfaced, which is a common and correctable planning gap, not a competence failure. A senior team member re-estimates collaboratively, using planning poker or a similar team technique, once the stories are properly split, rather than overriding the estimate unilaterally.

The response should also note the broader behavior being modeled for the team: a senior person makes unknowns visible early in grooming rather than letting the team discover them mid-sprint, and treats precise, honestly-scoped story splitting as part of their responsibility to the sprint's predictability, not just a nice-to-have.
questions.professionalAnswer:
In grooming, I'd just say out loud, 'I don't think this is one story — I think there are at least three stories hiding inside it.' I'd split it: one story to pin down the actual CLV formula with Product, because 'lifetime value' means five different things depending on who you ask; one to confirm the data sources actually have what we need and are joinable; one for the underlying model and measures; and one for the dashboard itself.

I'd be careful not to make the junior analyst feel called out for the 3-point estimate — I'd frame it as, 'this was estimated before we knew about the unknowns in the calculation logic, which is totally normal, that's exactly what grooming is for.' Then I'd have the team re-estimate each piece together once it's split, rather than me just overriding his number myself. Honestly, the biggest thing I'm modeling here for the team is that surfacing unknowns in grooming, before the sprint starts, is a core part of the job — not something you only do when something breaks mid-sprint.
questions.example: Split: (1) Validate CLV calculation logic with Product, (2) Confirm/connect data sources, (3) Build semantic model & measures, (4) Build dashboard visualization — each separately estimated.
commonMistakes: Accepting a vague, oversized story as a single sprint item without decomposing it
Silently re-estimating the story unilaterally instead of involving the team
Publicly undermining the junior analyst's original estimate instead of framing it as a normal grooming gap
Not surfacing the calculation-logic ambiguity ('lifetime value' meaning) before committing to the sprint
Letting unknowns about data source validity go unaddressed until mid-sprint discovery
keyPoints: Decomposes a vague, oversized backlog item into independently valuable, estimable stories
Surfaces calculation and data-source unknowns during grooming, not mid-sprint
Reframes the original estimate's gap constructively rather than as a mistake by the junior analyst
Facilitates collaborative team re-estimation rather than overriding unilaterally
Models proactive unknown-surfacing as a senior responsibility within the Scrum process

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly identifies and decomposes the oversized/ambiguous story into discrete, estimable stories
Surfaces calculation logic and data source unknowns proactively during grooming
Handles the junior analyst's original estimate constructively and respectfully
Uses collaborative, team-based re-estimation rather than unilateral override
Demonstrates understanding of how senior ownership operates within the Scrum process

questions.title: Pushing Back on Mid-Sprint Scope Creep on a Dashboard User Story
questions.prompt: Three days into a two-week sprint, the Product Owner messages you asking to add two new filter dimensions and a drill-through page to a dashboard user story your team already committed to and sized at the sprint's start. She frames it as 'small additions.' Your team is on track to meet the original commitment but adding this would jeopardize that. As the senior BI person others look to for how to handle this, what do you do?
questions.modelAnswer:
A strong answer treats this as a textbook mid-sprint scope protection moment, and models the correct Scrum behavior for the rest of the team rather than just solving it quietly themselves. The candidate should first assess honestly whether the additions really are small or whether 'small additions' is underselling the actual work (new filter dimensions typically require model changes, not just visual tweaks, and a drill-through page is a materially new deliverable) — and should say so plainly rather than accepting the framing uncritically.

The response should describe declining to silently absorb the scope change into the current sprint, instead offering the Product Owner a clear choice: add the new items to the backlog for the next sprint with proper estimation, or, if there's a true urgent business reason it must happen now, negotiate explicitly what gets removed or deferred from the current sprint to make room — making the tradeoff visible rather than letting the team silently absorb unplanned work and risk the whole sprint's commitment.

A senior answer also addresses team dynamics: communicating this decision transparently to the team so junior members see that sprint commitments are protected deliberately, not just hoped for, and that saying 'let's scope this for next sprint' is a normal, healthy part of the process rather than a failure to be agile.
questions.professionalAnswer:
I'd push back right away, but not harshly — I'd say, 'Those aren't actually small. New filter dimensions usually mean model changes, not just UI tweaks, and a drill-through page is basically a new deliverable on its own. Let's not pretend this fits inside what we already committed to.' I wouldn't just quietly try to squeeze it in and hope the team absorbs it, because that's exactly how a sprint commitment turns into nobody trusting sprint commitments.

Then I'd give her the real choice: 'I can add both to the backlog for next sprint and we'll estimate them properly, or if this genuinely can't wait, tell me what you want to cut from the current sprint to make room — I'm not going to have the team just quietly work nights to fit it in.' Honestly, I think the most important part of handling this is doing it visibly, in front of the team, not just in a DM with the PO — because the newer folks on my team need to see that protecting the sprint commitment is a deliberate, normal thing a senior person does, not some rare act of defiance.
questions.example: Response to PO: 'Those two filters and the drill-through aren't small — they're more like a model change plus a new page. Backlog them for next sprint, or tell me what to cut from this one to make room.'
commonMistakes: Accepting the 'small additions' framing uncritically without assessing the real scope impact
Silently absorbing the extra work into the sprint without renegotiating the commitment
Not making the tradeoff (what gets cut or deferred) explicit and visible to the Product Owner
Handling the pushback privately instead of modeling the behavior transparently for the team
Treating 'no, let's backlog this' as a failure of agility rather than a normal part of sprint discipline
keyPoints: Accurately assesses whether 'small additions' genuinely are small before responding
Declines to silently absorb unplanned scope into an already-committed sprint
Offers a clear choice: backlog for next sprint, or explicit trade-off within current sprint
Makes the scope/trade-off conversation visible rather than handling it quietly alone
Models healthy sprint-commitment protection behavior for junior team members

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Accurately assesses the real scope impact rather than accepting the 'small' framing
Protects the sprint commitment rather than silently absorbing new scope
Offers the Product Owner a clear, explicit choice/trade-off
Handles the situation transparently in a way that models good practice for the team
Maintains a collaborative, non-adversarial tone with the Product Owner

questions.title: What a Senior BI Engineer Owns Differently in Release Management
questions.prompt: Your team follows a Dev/QA/UAT/Production promotion process with scheduled releases for dashboard and dataset changes. A junior analyst asks you, 'Why do you get involved in release planning meetings and change approval boards when I just push my changes through QA and wait for sign-off?' How do you explain what a senior BI person owns differently in this release process, and demonstrate it with a specific example?
questions.modelAnswer:
A strong answer distinguishes individual-contributor responsibility (getting one's own change correctly through Dev, QA, and UAT) from senior ownership of the release as a whole system of interacting changes and business risk. The candidate should explain that a senior BI person in the change approval board is evaluating cross-change interactions a junior analyst focused on a single change wouldn't see — for example, catching that their own dataset refactor scheduled for this release will conflict with another analyst's report change going out the same day because both touch the same shared dimension table, and that conflict wouldn't surface in either person's individual UAT testing.

The response should also cover timing and business-risk judgment: a senior person weighs release timing against business calendar risk (e.g., not deploying model changes to executive dashboards the day before quarter-end close) in ways that require broader context than any single ticket carries, and owns the rollback plan and communication plan for a release, not just the change itself.

Finally, the answer should frame this as a growth path for the junior analyst, not a permanent gatekeeping distinction — explaining what experience and context (seeing more releases, more incidents, more cross-team dependencies) builds the judgment to eventually sit in those same rooms, and perhaps inviting the junior analyst to shadow the next change approval board meeting as a concrete next step.
questions.professionalAnswer:
I'd tell him the honest difference is scope, not status. 'When you push a change through QA, you're making sure your change is correct. When I sit on the change approval board, I'm checking whether your change and three other people's changes, all going out in the same release, interact badly with each other — which none of you would catch in your own individual UAT.' And I'd give him a real example: 'Last release, your dataset refactor and Priya's report change both touched the shared customer dimension table. Neither of your individual tests would've caught that, because you were each only looking at your own piece.'

I'd also point out the stuff that's easy to miss when you're focused on one ticket — like not scheduling a model change to the exec dashboard the day before quarter-end close, or making sure there's an actual rollback plan if something breaks, not just hoping it doesn't. And I'd end on, 'This isn't a permanent wall between us — it's exactly the kind of judgment you build by seeing more releases and more of what goes wrong. Come sit in on the next change approval board with me, you'll pick it up fast.'
questions.example: Example cited: a dataset refactor and a separate report change both modifying the same shared dimension table in the same release — invisible in either individual's UAT, caught only at the release-level review.
commonMistakes: Framing the difference as seniority/status rather than genuine difference in scope of responsibility
Not providing a concrete, specific example of a cross-change risk individual testing wouldn't catch
Omitting business-calendar timing judgment (e.g., avoiding risky releases near quarter-end) from the explanation
Failing to mention rollback/communication plan ownership as part of release-level responsibility
Presenting the distinction as a permanent gatekeeping barrier rather than a growth path for the junior analyst
keyPoints: Distinguishes individual change correctness from release-level, cross-change ownership
Gives a concrete example of a cross-change conflict invisible to individual UAT testing
Covers business-calendar timing judgment as part of senior release responsibility
Includes ownership of rollback and communication plans, not just the technical change
Frames the distinction as a growth path, inviting the junior analyst to build toward it

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Clearly distinguishes individual change ownership from release-level/cross-change ownership
Provides a concrete, specific example illustrating the difference
Covers business-risk/timing judgment and rollback/communication ownership
Frames the explanation as a growth path rather than permanent gatekeeping
Communicates respectfully in a way that supports the junior analyst's development

questions.title: Why Indexing Layers Like The Graph Exist
questions.prompt: A blockchain's RPC interface gives you block, transaction, and receipt lookups by key, not a relational database. Explain concretely why a dApp frontend can't just run something equivalent to 'SELECT * FROM transfers WHERE from = X ORDER BY amount DESC' against a node, and what specific problem a subgraph / The Graph indexing layer solves that raw RPC calls can't solve efficiently. Give one concrete query that would be essentially infeasible to serve directly from a node.
questions.modelAnswer: An RPC node exposes access by known key: give it a block number, a transaction hash, or a contract address plus storage slot, and it returns a value. It has no concept of 'find all events matching this filter, sorted and aggregated' the way a relational database does. The closest primitive, eth_getLogs, lets you filter logs by contract address and topics, but it operates over a bounded block range (most providers cap this at a few thousand blocks per call), returns raw undecoded log data, and performs no sorting, joining, or aggregation. To answer something like 'every NFT sale by address X in the last year, sorted by price,' a client would have to decode the contract's full event ABI, paginate eth_getLogs calls across the entire block range in small chunks, decode every matching log client-side, and sort/aggregate the results in application code — for popular contracts this means scanning millions of logs on every page load. A subgraph solves this by defining a schema of entities (Transfer, Sale, Listing) and mapping handlers that run as each block is indexed, transforming raw event logs into structured, relational records in an off-chain database the moment they occur. That database is then queried through GraphQL with native filtering, sorting, pagination, and entity relationships, turning what would be a chain-wide log scan into a single indexed query.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd start by pointing out that an RPC node isn't a database — it's a key-value lookup. You ask for block N, or the receipt for tx hash H, or the storage at a given slot, and you get exactly that back, nothing more. There's no WHERE clause. The closest thing, eth_getLogs, will filter by address and topic, but providers cap how many blocks you can scan in one call, and even then you just get raw, undecoded logs back — you still have to decode and aggregate them yourself in your app. So if someone asks 'show me all this wallet's NFT sales from the past year, cheapest first,' doing that live against a node means paging through the entire chain's logs in small chunks, decoding each one, and sorting in memory — that's slow, rate-limited, and basically unworkable for a production frontend. What The Graph does is flip the timing: instead of scanning history on demand, a subgraph's mapping handlers watch events as blocks land and write them into structured entities in real time. By the time your frontend asks the question, it's not scanning anything — it's running an indexed GraphQL query against data that's already shaped the way you need it, with sorting and filtering built in.
questions.example: Query: 'all Sale events for seller 0xABC in the last 90 days, sorted by price descending.' Via raw RPC this means paginating eth_getLogs across ~650,000 blocks in provider-sized chunks and decoding every log client-side; via a subgraph it's a single GraphQL query like `sales(where: {seller: "0xABC", timestamp_gt: X}, orderBy: price, orderDirection: desc)`.
commonMistakes: Assuming eth_getLogs supports arbitrary filtering, joins, or aggregation like SQL
Not knowing eth_getLogs block ranges are capped by RPC providers, forcing pagination for any historical scan
Believing on-chain storage can be queried by anything other than a known key or slot
Underestimating the cost of re-deriving aggregates (totals, rankings, counts) client-side on every page load
Confusing an indexing problem (The Graph) with an off-chain data problem (oracles)
keyPoints: RPC access is key-based lookup, not relational querying
eth_getLogs is bounded by block range and returns undecoded, unsorted data
Subgraphs index events into structured entities via mapping handlers as blocks arrive
GraphQL on top of a subgraph provides filtering, sorting, pagination, and relationships
Historical/aggregate queries become a single fast query instead of a chain-wide scan

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly explains why RPC nodes are not queryable like a relational database
Correctly describes eth_getLogs limitations (block range caps, no aggregation)
Explains how subgraph mapping handlers pre-index events into entities
Gives a concrete, infeasible-without-an-indexer example query

questions.title: The Oracle Problem and Chainlink's Mitigation
questions.prompt: Explain the 'oracle problem' — why smart contracts cannot natively and trustlessly access off-chain data like asset prices — and the specific manipulation risk that a naive single-source price feed introduces. Then explain, mechanically, how Chainlink's decentralized oracle network design (independent node operators, aggregation, deviation thresholds, heartbeat updates) mitigates that risk without fully eliminating the need for trust.
questions.modelAnswer: A blockchain's execution environment is deterministic and isolated by design: every node must arrive at the same state given the same inputs, so a smart contract cannot make an HTTP call to an exchange API directly — doing so would make consensus impossible, since different nodes could observe different values at different times. The 'oracle problem' is the resulting gap: any off-chain fact (a price, a weather outcome, a sports result) has to be pushed on-chain by some external actor, and that actor becomes a trusted intermediary unless its design is scrutinized. A naive implementation — one contract call to one centralized price source — creates a single point of manipulation: if that source can be bribed, hacked, or simply has a thin, illiquid market, an attacker can move the reported price and profit against any protocol relying on it (classic flash-loan-driven oracle manipulation attacks exploited exactly this on protocols reading spot price from a single low-liquidity DEX pool). Chainlink mitigates this by decentralizing both the source and the reporting path: a price feed aggregates independently operated, reputationally staked node operators who each pull from multiple off-chain exchanges/data providers, submit their observations, and have those observations aggregated (typically via median) on-chain, so no single node's bad report moves the final value. Updates are triggered either by a heartbeat (a maximum time since the last update) or by a deviation threshold (price moved more than X%), balancing gas cost against freshness. This raises the cost of manipulation from 'compromise one source' to 'collude a majority of independent, staked operators across diverse data sources' — a meaningfully higher bar, though it does not make the feed perfectly trustless, since you are still trusting the economic security and honesty of the oracle network's design and operators.
questions.professionalAnswer: The core issue is that a blockchain has to be deterministic — every validator needs to agree on the exact same state, so a contract literally cannot go fetch a price from an exchange's API itself, because different nodes would see different answers at different times and consensus would break. So someone has to bring that data in from outside, and whoever does that is a trust bottleneck unless you've designed around it. If you just wire a contract to one price source, you've basically built a single point of failure — we saw this play out for real with flash-loan attacks where someone temporarily drains or distorts a thin on-chain pool, reads a manipulated spot price off it in the same transaction, and profits before anyone can react. The way Chainlink deals with this is by spreading the trust across multiple independent, economically staked operators who each go pull data from several exchanges, not just one, and then the final on-chain value is an aggregate — usually a median — of all those independent submissions, so one bad or bribed node barely moves the result. They also don't update on every tiny price tick; they update either on a heartbeat timer or when the price moves past a deviation threshold, which keeps gas costs sane while still guaranteeing freshness. I'd be honest in an interview that this reduces the attack surface a lot — you'd need to compromise a majority of independent operators pulling from diverse sources, which is expensive — but it's not magic; you're still trusting the design and incentive structure of that oracle network, not achieving some perfectly trustless state.
questions.example: A lending protocol reading spot price directly from a single low-liquidity Uniswap pool can be manipulated within one flash-loaned transaction; a Chainlink feed aggregating median prices from many independent nodes pulling from many exchanges is far more expensive to move, since an attacker would need to corrupt a majority of those independent sources simultaneously.
commonMistakes: Thinking smart contracts could technically call an external API if developers just wrote the code for it
Assuming decentralized oracles are fully trustless rather than meaningfully trust-minimized
Not connecting single-source price reads to real flash-loan oracle manipulation exploits
Confusing heartbeat and deviation-threshold update triggers, or omitting the gas-cost tradeoff they balance
Describing Chainlink aggregation without mentioning that it's specifically resistant to any single operator's bad data
keyPoints: Blockchains are deterministic/isolated and cannot natively fetch off-chain data
A single-source price feed is a single point of manipulation (e.g. flash-loan attacks)
Chainlink aggregates independent, staked node operators pulling from multiple sources
On-chain values are typically a median, resisting any one bad report
Updates trigger on heartbeat or deviation threshold, trading gas cost against freshness

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly explains why blockchains cannot natively access off-chain data
Correctly identifies the manipulation risk of a single-source feed
Explains Chainlink's decentralized aggregation across independent operators
Explains heartbeat/deviation-threshold update mechanics
Acknowledges the mitigation reduces but does not eliminate trust

questions.title: Sign-In With Ethereum, End to End
questions.prompt: Walk through exactly what happens, end to end, when a user authenticates to a backend using Sign-In With Ethereum (EIP-4361). Cover the structure of the signed message, why a server-issued nonce is required, and precisely what a valid signature does and does not prove about the signer. Then contrast this with a traditional username/password login — what responsibility moves from the server to the user's wallet?
questions.modelAnswer: SIWE authentication begins with the backend generating a cryptographically random, single-use nonce and handing it to the client, usually alongside other required fields of the EIP-4361 message format: the domain requesting sign-in, the user's address, a statement describing what they're agreeing to, chain ID, issued-at timestamp, and optionally an expiration time. The frontend asks the wallet to sign this exact, human-readable plaintext message (not a transaction — no gas is spent, nothing touches the chain) using the wallet's private key via a personal_sign-style call. The signature, the message, and the claimed address are sent back to the server, which recovers the address from the signature using ECDSA recovery (ecrecover) and checks that the recovered address matches the claimed address, that the nonce matches one it issued and hasn't already been consumed, and that the message hasn't expired. The nonce is required specifically to prevent replay attacks: without it, an attacker who intercepts a previously valid signed message could resubmit it to authenticate as the user indefinitely, since the signature itself never expires on its own. A valid signature proves the possessor of that private key authorized that exact message at the time of signing — it proves control of the private key, nothing more. It does not prove the person signing is a particular human, that the wallet wasn't compromised, or that the user intends anything beyond what the message's literal text states (which is why the readable 'statement' field matters — a user should be able to understand what they're signing). Compared to username/password, the server no longer stores or verifies any secret of the user's; the burden of custody shifts entirely to the user's wallet and key management, and the server's job becomes purely cryptographic verification plus nonce/session bookkeeping.
questions.professionalAnswer: So the flow starts with my backend generating a one-time random nonce and sending it down, because that nonce is going to go into the message the wallet signs. The frontend builds an EIP-4361 formatted message — domain, address, a plain-English statement of what they're agreeing to, chain ID, issued-at time, and that nonce — and asks the wallet to sign it, which is just a signature, not a transaction, so there's no gas and nothing hits the chain. I get back the signature plus the message, and on the server I recover the address from the signature with ecrecover and check three things: does the recovered address match who they claim to be, does the nonce match one I actually issued and haven't used yet, and is the message still within whatever expiry I set. The nonce is the part people skip and shouldn't — without it, someone who captures a valid signed message once could just replay it forever to log in as that user, because a signature by itself never 'expires.' Now, what does a valid signature actually prove? Just that whoever holds that private key authorized exactly that message, at that moment. That's it. It doesn't prove a real human was at the keyboard, it doesn't prove the wallet wasn't compromised, and it definitely doesn't prove anything beyond the literal text of the message — which is exactly why that human-readable statement field matters, so a user isn't tricked into signing something they didn't understand. Compared to password auth, the big shift is that my server stops being a secrets vault — I'm not storing a password hash anymore. All the custody risk moves onto the user's own key management, and my job becomes pure signature verification plus making sure nonces can't be reused.
questions.example: A phishing site that convinces a user to sign a SIWE message for 'evil.com' as the domain field would produce a technically valid signature, but a correctly implemented server checks the domain field against its own expected value and rejects it — illustrating that signature validity alone isn't sufficient without checking every bound field.
commonMistakes: Treating SIWE signing as a transaction that costs gas, rather than an off-chain message signature
Omitting the nonce and not explaining the replay attack it prevents
Overstating what a signature proves (e.g. claiming it verifies human identity rather than key control)
Forgetting to check that the domain/expiration fields in the signed message match server expectations
Not explaining what responsibility shifts from server to wallet compared to password auth
keyPoints: Server issues a random single-use nonce before signing occurs
The wallet signs a structured EIP-4361 plaintext message, not a transaction
Server recovers the address via ecrecover and validates address, nonce, and expiry
A valid signature proves private key control at signing time, nothing about identity or intent beyond the message text
Custody responsibility shifts from server-held secrets to user-held keys

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly describes the EIP-4361 message structure and signing step
Correctly explains server-side verification via ecrecover and nonce checking
Explains why the nonce is required (replay prevention)
Accurately states what a signature does and does not prove
Contrasts responsibility shift versus traditional password authentication

questions.title: Constant-Product AMM Pricing and Slippage
questions.prompt: Explain how a constant-product AMM (x*y=k) derives a swap price purely from the invariant, with no order book. Then explain mechanically why a trade that is large relative to pool depth produces disproportionately worse execution price than a small trade — why slippage grows nonlinearly, not linearly, with trade size.
questions.modelAnswer: A constant-product AMM maintains two reserves, x and y, for a token pair, and enforces that their product k = x * y remains constant (ignoring fees) across any swap. There is no order book or matched counterparty; price is derived implicitly as the ratio of reserves, dy/dx, which is the pool's instantaneous marginal price. When a trader sends an amount of token X into the pool, the contract computes how much Y must leave to keep x*y = k constant: if a trader deposits dx, the new x reserve is x + dx, and the new y reserve must satisfy (x + dx)(y - dy) = k, solving to dy = y - k/(x + dx). Because k/(x+dx) is a nonlinear (hyperbolic) function of dx, the amount of Y received per unit of X put in shrinks as dx grows — the function is convex, so each additional unit of X contributed buys proportionally less Y than the unit before it, at a rate that accelerates. Intuitively, a trade that is tiny relative to reserves barely moves the ratio, so the execution price is close to the pre-trade marginal price; a trade that is a large fraction of the pool measurably depletes one side of the reserve, pushing the ratio — and thus the effective price for the marginal unit near the end of the trade — far from where it started. This is why slippage is quoted as a function of trade size relative to pool depth, not an absolute amount: the same absolute trade size causes far worse slippage in a shallow pool than a deep one, and doubling trade size in the same pool more than doubles the realized slippage.
questions.professionalAnswer: The way I'd frame it: there's no order book here, there's just two reserves and a rule that their product has to stay constant, ignoring fees for a second. So if I want to swap token X for token Y, the contract isn't matching me against another trader's order — it's solving an equation. I put in dx of X, and the new X reserve is x+dx, and it has to figure out how much Y to let out so that (x+dx) times the new Y reserve still equals the same k as before. Rearranging that, the Y I get out is y minus k over (x+dx) — and that k/(x+dx) term is a curve, not a straight line, so as dx gets bigger, the Y I'm getting per unit of X I put in keeps shrinking, and it shrinks faster and faster the bigger my trade gets relative to the pool. That's really the whole slippage story in one line: it's not that big trades get a slightly worse price, it's that the price degradation accelerates because you're moving along a curve, not a line. So if I size a trade that's, say, 1% of pool depth, I barely feel it — my execution price is basically the pool's current ratio. But if I try to push through a trade that's 30% of pool depth, I'm way out on that curve and getting crushed on price, and if I double that trade size I'm not paying twice the slippage, I'm paying a lot more than twice. That's exactly why depth matters so much when people quote AMM liquidity — the same dollar trade can be a non-event in a deep pool and devastating in a shallow one.
questions.example: A pool with 100 ETH and 200,000 USDC (k = 20,000,000). Swapping in 1 ETH yields roughly 1,980 USDC (~0.99% below the 2,000 spot rate). Swapping in 50 ETH (half the pool's ETH reserve) yields only about 66,667 USDC total — an average price far worse than 2,000/ETH, because the trade materially shifted the reserve ratio partway through its own execution.
commonMistakes: Describing AMM pricing as if it works like a matched order book
Treating slippage as a fixed percentage regardless of trade size relative to pool depth
Assuming slippage scales linearly with trade size instead of accelerating (convex curve)
Forgetting that the invariant (x*y=k) is what determines output, not a quoted price the pool 'looks up'
Ignoring that pool depth, not just trade size in absolute terms, determines execution quality
keyPoints: Price is the implicit ratio of reserves (dy/dx), not an order-book match
Swap output dy is solved from keeping x*y=k constant after adding dx
The output function is nonlinear/convex in trade size, not linear
Slippage accelerates as trade size grows relative to pool depth
The same absolute trade size produces worse slippage in a shallower pool

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly explains that price is derived from the reserve ratio, not an order book
Correctly derives/describes the swap output formula from the invariant
Explains why the output function is nonlinear/convex in input size
Connects pool depth to the severity of slippage for a given trade size

questions.title: Impermanent Loss Without Any Hack or Exploit
questions.prompt: Explain why a liquidity provider in a constant-product pool can end up with less total value than if they had simply held the two underlying assets separately — even with zero hacks, zero rug pulls, and the protocol working exactly as designed. Walk through the mechanics of why the pool's automatic rebalancing causes this, and identify the specific price-movement condition under which impermanent loss is worst.
questions.modelAnswer: Impermanent loss arises purely from the arbitrage mechanism that keeps an AMM pool's internal price aligned with the external market price. When an LP deposits assets, they receive a share of the pool's reserves at the current ratio. If the external market price of one asset moves, arbitrageurs will trade against the pool — buying the now-relatively-cheap asset from the pool and selling the now-relatively-expensive one into it — until the pool's reserve ratio reflects the new external price. Because the pool must always satisfy x*y=k, this arbitrage mechanically changes the composition of what the LP's share represents: the pool ends up holding more of the asset that fell in price and less of the asset that rose in price, because arbitrageurs extracted the appreciating asset from the pool in exchange for the depreciating one. This means the LP's position automatically rebalances away from the winning asset and toward the losing one, exactly the opposite of what a simple buy-and-hold position would do. The LP still collects trading fees, which can offset this, but the underlying mechanics guarantee that absent any fee income, a pool position is worth less than holding the two assets separately whenever their relative price has diverged in either direction from the price at deposit time — it is 'impermanent' only in the sense that it disappears if the price returns exactly to the deposit-time ratio before withdrawal. Impermanent loss is worst when the divergence between the two assets' price is large and one-directional (e.g., one asset doubles or triples relative to the other), since the magnitude of loss relative to holding grows with the square of the price ratio change, not linearly.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd explain it by walking through what actually happens mechanically, because that's where the 'aha' is. When I deposit into a pool, I own a slice of whatever's in those reserves at that moment. Now say the external market price of one of those assets moves — doesn't matter which direction. Arbitrageurs are going to come in and trade against the pool specifically to pull its internal price back in line with the market, because that price gap is free money for them. The thing is, arbitrage only happens in one direction given a price move: they buy the asset that's now underpriced in the pool and dump the overpriced one into it. So the pool ends up accumulating more of whatever just went down in value and less of whatever just went up — which is exactly backwards from what I'd want if I were just holding both assets myself. That's the whole mechanism, no exploit required, just the pool doing its job of staying arbitrage-free. Fees I earn as an LP can offset this, sometimes fully, but strip the fees away and the math is unforgiving: any price divergence in either direction leaves me worse off than if I'd just held. And it gets worse fast, not linearly — if one asset goes up 4x relative to the other, I'm not down a proportional little bit, I'm down a lot, because the loss scales roughly with the square of how far the ratio has moved. It's called 'impermanent' because if the price round-trips back to where it was when I deposited, the loss vanishes — but if I withdraw while prices have diverged, that loss is very much realized and permanent for me.
questions.example: An LP deposits into an ETH/USDC pool when ETH = $2,000. If ETH later quadruples to $8,000 and the LP withdraws at that point, the LP's position is worth meaningfully less than if they had simply held their original ETH and USDC separately, even though no hack occurred — because arbitrage continually sold the pool's ETH into USDC as the price rose, leaving the LP's share holding more USDC and less of the asset that appreciated.
commonMistakes: Assuming impermanent loss requires a hack, exploit, or malicious actor
Thinking impermanent loss only occurs when price moves in one specific direction rather than either direction
Forgetting that trading fees earned can partially or fully offset impermanent loss
Describing the loss as scaling linearly with price divergence instead of accelerating
Confusing impermanent loss with simply 'the price went down,' rather than underperformance versus holding
keyPoints: Arbitrage, not any exploit, drives the pool's reserve ratio back to the external market price
Arbitrage mechanically shifts the pool toward holding more of the depreciating asset
LP composition rebalances opposite to what a buy-and-hold position would do
Fees can offset impermanent loss but the underlying mechanics still apply
Loss grows faster than linearly with the magnitude of price divergence

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly explains that arbitrage against the pool, not a hack, causes the effect
Correctly explains the reserve rebalancing mechanism and its direction
Identifies the condition under which IL is worst (large price divergence)
Notes the role of fees in offsetting (but not eliminating) the mechanical loss

questions.title: Why Lending Protocols Overcollateralize Instead of Trusting Credit
questions.prompt: Explain the mechanics of overcollateralized lending: what a collateral factor (or LTV cap) is, how a position's health factor is calculated, and why DeFi lending protocols require collateral to exceed the borrowed value rather than extending credit based on identity or reputation the way a traditional bank would.
questions.modelAnswer: A traditional bank extends unsecured or under-secured credit because it has legal recourse: identity verification, credit history, contracts enforceable in court, and the ability to pursue a defaulting borrower. A DeFi lending protocol has none of those tools — a borrower's on-chain address carries no enforceable legal identity, and if they simply walk away from a loan, the protocol cannot sue them or garnish wages. The only enforcement mechanism available is purely economic and automated: the protocol must hold collateral it can seize and liquidate programmatically, and that collateral must be worth more than the loan at all times to absorb price volatility between the moment a position becomes under-collateralized and the moment a liquidator actually executes the liquidation. This is implemented via a collateral factor (sometimes called loan-to-value or LTV cap) per asset — e.g., ETH might have an 80% collateral factor, meaning $100 of ETH collateral can back at most $80 of borrowing. The health factor is a running ratio, typically (collateral value * liquidation threshold) / borrowed value; a health factor above 1 means the position is safely collateralized, and a health factor at or below 1 means the position is eligible for liquidation, at which point a liquidator can repay some or all of the debt in exchange for a discounted claim on the collateral, usually earning a liquidation bonus/penalty for doing so. Because this entire mechanism is automated and trustless, it must assume the worst case — a borrower who never repays and whose collateral value could suddenly drop — which is only safe if collateral is required to exceed debt by a margin wide enough to be liquidated before the collateral's value falls below the debt itself.
questions.professionalAnswer: The honest answer is that DeFi lending protocols overcollateralize because they have no other option — they can't do what a bank does. A bank can run a credit check, verify your identity, and ultimately sue you or come after your wages if you default. A smart contract talking to an anonymous address has none of that. There's no 'identity' to repossess from, so the only lever the protocol has is purely mechanical: hold collateral, and make sure that collateral is worth enough that it can be seized and sold off automatically before the debt becomes unrecoverable. That's where collateral factor comes in — each asset gets capped at some percentage of its value that it can be borrowed against, so if ETH has an 80% collateral factor, every $100 of ETH I deposit only lets me borrow up to $80 against it. Then there's the health factor, which is basically a live risk dial — collateral value times the liquidation threshold, divided by what I currently owe. As long as that number's comfortably above 1, I'm fine. The second it drops to 1 or below, I'm eligible to get liquidated — someone else can step in, pay off some or all of my debt, and take a discounted chunk of my collateral as a reward for doing so. The reason the margins have to be generous isn't arbitrary — it's because there's a real-world delay between a position crossing that threshold and a liquidator actually executing on-chain, and in that window the market can keep moving against the position. If the buffer's too thin, the protocol ends up with bad debt it has no legal way to recover. So overcollateralization isn't a design preference, it's the only enforcement mechanism available when there's no court system backing you up.
questions.example: A borrower deposits $150 of ETH with an 80% collateral factor, allowing up to $120 borrowed. If they borrow $100 in USDC, their health factor starts well above 1. If ETH's price drops such that the $150 collateral falls to $115, the health factor drops toward 1 and the position becomes eligible for liquidation before collateral value can fall below the $100 owed.
commonMistakes: Explaining overcollateralization as a conservative choice rather than the only enforcement mechanism available
Confusing collateral factor (borrowing capacity) with liquidation threshold (the point of forced liquidation)
Miscalculating or omitting one of the three terms in the health factor ratio
Forgetting that liquidators are economically incentivized via a discount/bonus to act promptly
Not explaining why the collateral buffer must absorb the delay between threshold breach and actual liquidation
keyPoints: DeFi protocols lack legal recourse against defaulting borrowers, unlike banks
Collateral factor/LTV cap limits how much can be borrowed against a given collateral value
Health factor = (collateral value * liquidation threshold) / borrowed value, roughly
A health factor at or below 1 makes a position eligible for liquidation
The collateral buffer must be wide enough to survive the delay before liquidation executes

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Explains why lack of legal recourse necessitates overcollateralization
Correctly defines collateral factor/LTV cap
Correctly describes the health factor calculation and its liquidation threshold
Explains the liquidator's economic incentive and the need for a volatility buffer

questions.title: Vesting Schedules, Cliffs, and Why Tokenomics Needs Them
questions.prompt: Explain why token allocations to a team and early investors typically use a vesting schedule with a cliff instead of transferring the full allocation immediately. Describe the mechanics of linear vesting versus a cliff, and explain what specific incentive-misalignment or market risk each mechanism is designed to prevent.
questions.modelAnswer: If team and investor tokens were fully liquid at launch, the people with the most information about the project's actual health and the least immediate need to sustain its price would have both the means and no deterrent to sell immediately — a scenario commonly called a 'dump,' which crashes price for every other holder and public buyer, destroys the project's credibility, and breaks the incentive alignment the token was supposed to create between founders and long-term success. Vesting solves this by locking the economic realization of the allocation to the passage of time (and sometimes milestones), ensuring that the people building the project only benefit if the token retains or grows value over a multi-year horizon, the same horizon over which they're expected to deliver. Mechanically, linear vesting releases tokens continuously (or in small discrete steps, e.g., monthly) over a defined total duration — e.g., 10,000 tokens vesting linearly over 48 months unlocks roughly 208.3 tokens per month. A cliff is a separate mechanism, usually layered at the start of a vesting schedule, during which zero tokens unlock regardless of elapsed time, followed by a lump-sum unlock at the cliff's end before linear vesting (if any) resumes — for example, a 12-month cliff on a 48-month schedule means nothing vests for the first year, then 25% unlocks at month 12, with the remaining 75% vesting linearly over the following 36 months. The cliff specifically protects against short-term contributors who might leave quickly: without it, someone could join, vest a small amount almost immediately, and leave with liquid tokens having delivered minimal value; the cliff forces a meaningful minimum commitment period before any value can be realized at all.
questions.professionalAnswer: The problem vesting solves is pretty blunt: if you hand the team and early investors their full token allocation on day one, you've just given the people with the most inside knowledge and the least skin-in-the-game-over-time every reason to sell immediately and no mechanism stopping them. That tanks the price on everyone else who bought in believing in the long-term story. Vesting fixes the incentive by tying when they can actually realize value to how long they stick around and keep the project healthy — so their payoff depends on the same multi-year outcome everyone else cares about. Mechanically there are really two separate levers here. Linear vesting just drips tokens out continuously or in small chunks over a set period — say 10,000 tokens over 48 months works out to roughly 208 tokens unlocking every month, nice and smooth. A cliff is a different thing entirely — it's a hard wall at the front where literally nothing unlocks, and then at the end of that period a chunk vests all at once before the linear drip (if there is one) kicks in. A typical setup is a 12-month cliff on a 4-year grant — year one, you get zero, then 25% vests in one shot at the 12-month mark, and the other 75% trickles out monthly over the remaining three years. The specific thing the cliff is guarding against is someone joining for a few months, picking up a token allocation that's already partially vested, and bailing with liquid tokens having barely contributed — the cliff makes sure nobody gets anything until they've proven out a real minimum commitment.
questions.example: A core engineer is granted 48,000 tokens on a 4-year schedule with a 1-year cliff. If they leave after 8 months, they receive zero tokens — nothing has vested yet. If they stay past the 12-month cliff, 12,000 tokens (25%) vest immediately, then the remaining 36,000 vest in equal monthly installments of 1,000 over the next 3 years.
commonMistakes: Describing vesting only as an anti-dump measure without connecting it to long-term incentive alignment
Confusing a cliff with just 'slow linear vesting' rather than a distinct zero-unlock period followed by a lump sum
Getting the monthly unlock arithmetic wrong for a given total amount and duration
Forgetting that the cliff specifically targets short-tenure departures, a different risk than the dump risk linear vesting addresses
Assuming all token holders (e.g. public sale buyers) are vested the same way as team/investors
keyPoints: Immediate full liquidity for insiders creates a sell-pressure/dump risk against informed, low-commitment holders
Vesting ties realized value to a multi-year time horizon matching expected contribution
Linear vesting releases tokens continuously/incrementally over a set duration
A cliff is a zero-unlock period followed by a lump-sum unlock before any further vesting
The cliff specifically deters short-tenure participants from capturing value with minimal commitment

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Explains the dump/incentive-misalignment risk that vesting addresses
Correctly describes linear vesting mechanics with a concrete calculation
Correctly describes cliff mechanics as distinct from linear vesting
Explains the specific risk a cliff mitigates (short-tenure departures)

questions.title: Why DAO Governance Needs a Timelock Before Execution
questions.prompt: A DAO proposal that passes a vote isn't executed immediately — it's queued into a timelock and only becomes executable after a delay. Explain the specific attack or risk scenario this delay protects against, and why a multisig or token-vote outcome alone, without a timelock, would be insufficient protection even if the vote itself was legitimate and uncontested.
questions.modelAnswer: A timelock enforces a mandatory delay between a governance proposal passing and its actual on-chain execution, and its primary purpose is to give the broader community — and especially any automated monitoring or security tooling watching the DAO's treasury and contract interactions — a guaranteed window to detect and react to a malicious or erroneous proposal before it takes effect. Even a 'legitimately passed' vote can be dangerous: governance token voting power is often concentrated, can be flash-loaned or temporarily acquired to swing a vote, or a proposal's payload (the actual encoded contract calls it will execute) can be crafted to look benign in its description while actually granting an attacker minting rights, draining a treasury, or upgrading a proxy to malicious logic. Without a timelock, execution would be instantaneous upon the vote passing, meaning by the time anyone notices something is wrong, the damage (funds drained, permissions changed) is already irreversible. With a timelock, if the DAO's monitoring, a watchdog multisig with veto/cancel power, or simply public scrutiny identifies the proposal as malicious during the delay window, the execution can be cancelled before it happens. This is also why a multisig alone, without a timelock, is insufficient even if its signers are honest and the vote legitimate: a compromised signer key, a social-engineering attack tricking signers into approving a malicious payload, or a legitimate-looking proposal with a hidden malicious encoded call all still execute immediately upon reaching signature threshold — the timelock is what converts 'irreversible the moment consensus is reached' into 'reviewable for a fixed window before it becomes irreversible,' which is a fundamentally different security property than requiring agreement alone.
questions.professionalAnswer: The way I think about a timelock is that it's not there to stop a vote from passing — it's there to create a mandatory pause between 'this passed' and 'this actually happens,' so there's a window where people can catch something before it's too late. And the risk it's guarding against is real even when the vote itself wasn't fraudulent. Governance voting power can be concentrated, or in the worst case temporarily borrowed — think flash-loaned governance tokens just long enough to swing a vote — and separately, a proposal's actual payload, the encoded calls it's going to execute, can say one thing in its human-readable description and do something completely different under the hood, like quietly granting mint rights or pointing a proxy at malicious logic. If execution happened the instant the vote passed, nobody gets a chance to catch that before the damage is done and irreversible. The timelock buys a window — hours or days — where a watchdog multisig with cancel power, security researchers, or honestly just anyone paying attention can look at exactly what's about to execute and pull the emergency brake if it's bad. And I'd specifically push back on the idea that a multisig alone solves this, even with totally honest signers: a signer's key can get phished or compromised, or signers can get socially engineered into approving something that looks fine on the surface but isn't — and without a timelock, the moment that threshold of signatures is hit, it's already executed. The timelock is what turns 'irreversible the second people agree' into 'there's a guaranteed review window before it's irreversible' — that's a genuinely different security guarantee than just trusting that the people who signed off were right.
questions.example: A malicious proposal titled 'Routine parameter update' actually encodes a call granting the proposer minting rights over the treasury token. If it passed and executed instantly, the exploit would be irreversible by the time anyone read the encoded calldata. With a 48-hour timelock, a monitoring bot or community member decoding the queued transaction can flag it and a guardian multisig can cancel it before execution.
commonMistakes: Assuming a timelock only matters if the vote itself was fraudulent or contested
Not distinguishing between a proposal's human-readable description and its actual encoded payload
Believing an honest multisig alone provides the same protection as a timelock
Forgetting that governance voting power can be temporarily acquired (e.g. via flash loans) to pass a bad vote
Treating the timelock delay as arbitrary rather than as a deliberate review/reaction window
keyPoints: A timelock creates a mandatory delay between a proposal passing and executing
The delay gives a window to detect malicious or mis-encoded proposal payloads
A proposal's description can misrepresent its actual encoded on-chain calls
A multisig without a timelock executes immediately on reaching signature threshold, with no review window
The timelock converts an irreversible-on-agreement action into a reviewable, cancellable one

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Explains the mandatory delay mechanism and its purpose
Identifies the specific risk of a malicious or mis-encoded payload passing a vote
Explains why a multisig alone, without a timelock, is insufficient
Connects the timelock to a concrete detection/cancellation mechanism

questions.title: Fuzz Testing vs. Invariant Testing: Different Questions
questions.prompt: Fuzz testing and invariant testing are both randomized testing techniques used heavily in Foundry, and both are necessary for auditing advanced smart contracts — but they answer fundamentally different questions. Explain precisely what question each one answers, why a contract that passes all its fuzz tests can still be exploitable, and give a concrete example of a bug that invariant testing would catch but fuzz testing on individual functions would not.
questions.modelAnswer: Fuzz testing answers the question 'does this one function behave correctly for a wide range of random inputs?' — a fuzz test calls a single function (or a tightly scoped set of calls within one test) with many randomly generated argument values, checking that the function's documented pre/post-conditions hold for each. It operates within a single call, essentially stress-testing input-space coverage for isolated logic like a math function or a single state transition. Invariant testing answers a different question entirely: 'does some global property of the system hold no matter what arbitrary SEQUENCE of valid calls, across potentially multiple functions and multiple actors, is made against it?' Foundry's invariant testing harness randomly selects functions to call (from a defined 'handler' contract) in random order with random arguments across many sequential calls, and after each call (or after the whole sequence) re-checks a property that should always hold — total supply equals sum of balances, a pool's k never decreases except via fees, or total shares always correspond to real collateral. A contract can pass every fuzz test on every individual function in isolation and still be exploitable, because the exploit may only manifest from a specific ORDER of calls across functions that individually behave correctly — for example, a reentrancy-adjacent bug where calling withdraw() then deposit() then withdraw() again in the same sequence leaves accounting inconsistent, even though withdraw() and deposit() each pass fuzzing perfectly on their own. A concrete example: a vault where each function individually enforces its own balance checks correctly, but calling flashLoan() followed immediately by deposit() within the same transaction sequence lets an attacker manipulate a share-price calculation that depends on a reserve balance invariant assumption no single-function fuzz test would ever construct, because fuzzing one function doesn't explore multi-call, multi-function sequences at all.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd draw the line like this: fuzz testing is asking 'if I throw a thousand random inputs at this one function, does it still hold up?' — it's great for catching edge cases in math-heavy logic, off-by-ones, overflow-adjacent bugs, stuff like that, but it's fundamentally testing one function in isolation, call by call. Invariant testing is asking a completely different question: 'no matter what crazy sequence of calls, across any of my functions, in any order, with any actors, does some property of my whole system still hold?' Foundry does this by picking random functions off a handler contract and calling them in random order with random args, over and over, and after all that chaos, checking that something like total supply equals the sum of all balances, or the pool's k value never drops outside of fee collection. The reason a contract can sail through every fuzz test and still get drained in production is that the bug isn't in any single function — it's in the interaction between functions, in a specific order nobody fuzzed for because fuzzing one function at a time never constructs multi-step sequences at all. The classic shape of this is something like: deposit, then flash-loan, then withdraw, all chained together in a way that lets someone manipulate a share price calculation that silently assumes a reserve balance nobody explicitly checked holds across that particular sequence. Each of those three functions passes fuzzing beautifully on its own — correct math, correct bounds checking — but invariant testing, which is specifically hammering on random call sequences and checking a global property after each one, is what would eventually stumble into that exact order and catch the property breaking.
questions.example: A lending vault's withdraw() function correctly fuzz-tests against any single random withdrawal amount. But an invariant test running random sequences of deposit(), borrow(), and withdraw() calls across multiple simulated users eventually constructs a sequence where total assets tracked on-chain diverge from the vault's real token balance — a bug only visible across a multi-call sequence, never visible fuzzing withdraw() alone.
commonMistakes: Treating fuzz testing and invariant testing as interchangeable or redundant
Assuming passing all fuzz tests on individual functions is sufficient coverage for a complex system
Describing invariant testing as just 'fuzzing with more inputs' rather than fuzzing call sequences
Not identifying that invariant bugs typically emerge from cross-function/cross-call-order interactions
Failing to give a concrete example distinguishing what each technique would or wouldn't catch
keyPoints: Fuzz testing checks one function's behavior across many random inputs
Invariant testing checks a global property across arbitrary sequences of randomized calls
Invariant testing explores multi-function, multi-call-order interactions fuzzing does not
A contract can pass all fuzz tests yet still have exploitable cross-call-sequence bugs
Advanced testing suites need both techniques because they catch different classes of bugs

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly defines what fuzz testing checks (single function, random inputs)
Correctly defines what invariant testing checks (global property, random call sequences)
Explains why passing fuzz tests doesn't guarantee a system-wide invariant holds
Gives a concrete, plausible example of a sequence-dependent bug

questions.title: Proxy Patterns: Where Logic and Storage Actually Live
questions.prompt: Explain how an upgradeable proxy pattern separates contract logic from contract storage — specifically, which contract's storage is actually used when a proxy delegatecalls into an implementation contract. Contrast the transparent proxy pattern with UUPS, and explain the storage-collision risk that makes a careless upgrade dangerous.
questions.modelAnswer: An upgradeable contract system splits a single logical contract into two deployed contracts: a proxy, which holds all persistent state and is the address users and other contracts actually interact with, and an implementation (or logic) contract, which holds the executable code but no meaningful persistent state of its own. The proxy forwards every call it receives to the implementation contract using delegatecall rather than a normal call; delegatecall executes the target's code but in the context of the CALLER's storage, meaning any SSTORE or SLOAD the implementation's code performs reads and writes the proxy's storage slots, not the implementation's. This is what allows 'upgrading': swapping which implementation address the proxy delegatecalls into changes the logic being executed while the proxy's storage — and therefore the state — remains untouched and continuous. The transparent proxy pattern keeps the upgrade logic (functions like upgradeTo()) inside the proxy contract itself, and resolves the ambiguity of what happens if an admin account calls a function that exists on both the proxy and the implementation by routing admin calls to the proxy's own logic and all other calls to the implementation — this adds a small amount of gas overhead on every call due to the caller-type check. UUPS (Universal Upgradeable Proxy Standard) instead puts the upgrade function inside the implementation contract itself, so the proxy becomes a minimal, gas-cheaper forwarder, at the cost of requiring every new implementation to remember to include the upgrade logic (an accidental omission can permanently brick upgradeability). The storage-collision risk arises because delegatecall reads/writes storage by SLOT NUMBER, not by variable name — if a new implementation's contract declares its state variables in a different order, or inserts a new variable earlier in the layout than a previous version did, the slot a given variable name used to occupy may now be occupied by a completely different variable, silently corrupting data (e.g., what used to be an 'owner' address slot might now be read as a 'balance' value). This is why upgradeable contracts enforce strict storage layout append-only discipline, and tools like OpenZeppelin's upgrades plugin specifically validate storage layout compatibility between versions before allowing an upgrade.
questions.professionalAnswer: The mental model I use is: there are two contracts, and only one of them actually matters for state. The proxy is the address everyone talks to and it's the only place storage lives in any meaningful sense. The implementation contract has code, but when the proxy calls into it, it uses delegatecall instead of a regular call, and delegatecall is the trick that makes this whole pattern work — it runs the implementation's code, but any storage read or write that code does happens against the CALLER's storage, which is the proxy's storage, not the implementation's own. So upgrading is just repointing which implementation address the proxy delegatecalls to — the data never moves, only the code being run against it changes. Now, transparent proxy versus UUPS is really about where the 'upgrade' function itself lives. Transparent proxies keep that logic in the proxy, and to avoid a weird edge case — what if an admin calls a function name that exists on both the proxy and the implementation — they just route any call from the admin account to the proxy's own functions and everyone else to the implementation. That adds a bit of gas overhead to every single call because it has to check who's calling. UUPS flips it: the upgrade function lives in the implementation, so the proxy itself is dead simple and cheap, but that means every single implementation you ever deploy has to remember to include that upgrade function, or you've just permanently bricked your ability to upgrade again. The storage collision risk is the part I'd really want to hammer on in an interview, because it's subtle and it's bitten real projects: storage in the EVM is addressed by slot number, it has no idea about your variable names. If version 2 of your implementation declares its variables in a different order than version 1 — say someone inserts a new variable above an existing one — slot 3 might have held 'owner' in v1 but now holds 'totalSupply' in v2, and nothing reverts, it just silently reads garbage. That's why the discipline around upgradeable contracts is strictly append-only for storage variables, and why tooling like OpenZeppelin's plugin actually diffs storage layouts between versions before letting an upgrade through.
questions.example: If implementation v1 declares `address owner;` at slot 0 and v2 mistakenly declares a new `uint256 fee;` before `address owner;`, fee now occupies slot 0 and owner occupies slot 1 — any code still expecting owner at slot 0 will silently misread the fee value as an address, corrupting access control without any revert.
commonMistakes: Thinking the implementation contract's own storage is used, rather than the proxy's, during delegatecall
Confusing delegatecall's storage context with a normal external call
Not knowing where the upgrade function lives in transparent proxy vs. UUPS, or the tradeoffs each implies
Believing storage collisions require a malicious actor rather than an innocent reordering of variables
Forgetting that storage is addressed by slot number, not by variable name, when reasoning about upgrade safety
keyPoints: The proxy holds all persistent storage; the implementation holds only code
delegatecall executes the implementation's code against the proxy's own storage
Transparent proxy keeps upgrade logic in the proxy and routes by caller type
UUPS keeps upgrade logic in the implementation, making the proxy cheaper but requiring every version to include it
Storage is addressed by slot number, so reordering variables between versions can silently corrupt data

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly explains that the proxy's storage, not the implementation's, is used via delegatecall
Correctly contrasts transparent proxy and UUPS upgrade-logic placement and tradeoffs
Correctly explains the storage-collision risk mechanism (slot-based addressing)
Notes the append-only/layout-validation discipline needed to upgrade safely

questions.title: Designing a Subgraph Schema for an NFT Marketplace
questions.prompt: Write a subgraph `schema.graphql` for an NFT marketplace that needs to track three things: token transfers, active listings, and completed sales. Define `Transfer`, `Listing`, and `Sale` entities with appropriate fields and relationships (e.g., a Sale should be able to reference the Listing it fulfilled). Briefly explain your field and relationship choices.
questions.modelAnswer: The schema should model each on-chain event as its own immutable entity where the event itself never changes after the fact (Transfer, Sale), while Listing is mutable because its `active` status changes over its lifecycle (created, then either fulfilled or cancelled). Transfer captures the raw ERC-721 Transfer event: tokenId, from, to, block timestamp, and transaction hash, with `id` typically set to the transaction hash plus log index to guarantee uniqueness across multiple transfers in one block. Listing captures a seller's intent to sell: seller address, tokenId, price, an `active` boolean (or status enum) flipped to false on sale or cancellation, and a createdAt timestamp — its id is naturally the on-chain listing ID if the contract assigns one, or a derived key otherwise. Sale is the critical entity for relationships: it should store a `listing: Listing!` reference (a one-to-one foreign-key-style relationship in GraphQL schema terms, resolved by `id`), plus buyer address, final price paid (which may differ from the listing's price if there was an auction/offer mechanism), and timestamp. This Sale-references-Listing relationship lets a query like 'show me this listing and the sale that fulfilled it, if any' resolve directly through the `sale` reverse-lookup field The Graph auto-generates from the forward reference, without needing to denormalize seller/tokenId data onto the Sale entity itself. Using Bytes for addresses and hashes (rather than String) is a performance/convention best practice in subgraph schemas since the underlying log data is already in that format.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd design this around which things are events-that-happened versus things-that-have-state. A Transfer and a Sale are both 'this happened at this block, it's never going to change' — so I'd mark both `@entity(immutable: true)`, which lets the Graph Node optimize storage since it never needs to check for updates to them. A Listing is different — it's created, then it's either still active, sold, or cancelled, so that one's mutable and I'd give it an `active` boolean I flip when it resolves. For the IDs, I'm using the transaction hash plus log index for Transfer and Sale, because a single block or even a single transaction could contain more than one of these events, and I need guaranteed uniqueness — just the tx hash alone isn't safe enough. The part I'd focus on explaining is the Sale-to-Listing link, because that's the relationship that makes the schema actually useful for querying. I give Sale a field like `listing: Listing!` pointing at the Listing it fulfilled, and the nice thing about The Graph's schema layer is it auto-generates a reverse lookup, so from a Listing I can query its fulfilling Sale without having to define that field myself on the Listing side. I'd keep buyer and final price on the Sale entity itself rather than trying to always read them back through the Listing, because if there's ever an auction or offer mechanism, the sale price might legitimately differ from the original listed price, and I don't want to lose that distinction. And small detail but I always use `Bytes!` for addresses and hashes instead of `String!` — it matches how the raw log data actually comes in and it's the standard convention in subgraph schemas.
questions.example:
type Sale @entity(immutable: true) {
  id: Bytes!
  listing: Listing!
  buyer: Bytes!
  price: BigInt!
  timestamp: BigInt!
}
Querying `listing { seller, sale { buyer, price } }` resolves the fulfilling sale directly from a listing via the auto-generated reverse lookup.
commonMistakes: Marking a mutable entity like Listing as immutable, preventing status updates
Using String instead of Bytes for addresses/hashes, against subgraph convention
Not guaranteeing unique entity IDs when multiple events can occur in the same block/transaction
Denormalizing all fields onto Sale instead of using a relationship reference to Listing
Forgetting to flip a Listing's active/status field when a Sale or cancellation occurs
keyPoints: Immutable entities for finalized events (Transfer, Sale); mutable entity for stateful Listing
Entity IDs must be unique even across multiple same-block events (tx hash + log index)
Sale references Listing via a typed field, enabling auto-generated reverse lookups
Bytes type used for addresses/hashes per subgraph convention
Sale stores its own final price separately from Listing's asking price to handle divergence
