questions.title: Writing an AssemblyScript Mapping Handler for a Transfer Event
questions.prompt: Write the AssemblyScript mapping handler function for a subgraph that listens for an ERC-721 `Transfer(address indexed from, address indexed to, uint256 indexed tokenId)` event. The handler should decode the event, create (or load and update) the relevant entity, and save it to the store. Explain why mapping handlers must load an existing entity before mutating it, rather than always constructing a new one.
questions.modelAnswer: A correct handler does two things: it records the immutable Transfer event itself, and it updates the mutable Token entity's current owner, which requires loading the existing Token entity (if one exists) rather than blindly instantiating a new one, since instantiating a new entity would overwrite any other fields already tracked on that token (e.g., metadata, listing status) with default/empty values. The implementation constructs a Transfer entity using a unique id (transaction hash concatenated with log index, since multiple transfers can occur in one transaction), sets from, to, tokenId, and timestamp from event.params and event.block, and calls .save(). For the Token entity, it calls Token.load(tokenId.toString()) first; if null (first time this token has been seen), it constructs a new Token entity, otherwise it mutates the loaded entity's owner field, then calls .save() either way. The reason loading-before-mutating is required in general (not just for this example) is that AssemblyScript entities are not a live reference to on-chain or stored state — each mapping invocation gets a fresh in-memory object, and calling `new Token(id)` always produces a blank entity with no field values, so any mapping handler that needs to preserve previously-stored fields on an entity across multiple events over that entity's lifetime must explicitly call `.load()` to retrieve the last-saved version before mutating and re-saving it; skipping this silently discards previously indexed data every time a new event touches that same entity.
questions.professionalAnswer: There are really two entities I'm touching here. First, the Transfer itself — that's just a historical record, so I build a brand new entity every time using the transaction hash plus the log index as the ID, since you can get multiple Transfer events in the same transaction and need that ID to stay unique. I pull from, to, and tokenId straight off event.params, grab the timestamp off event.block, and save it. The part that actually needs care is the Token entity, because that's the thing with ongoing state — it has an owner that needs to track the latest transfer. Here's the thing I'd flag immediately: I never just do `new Token(id)` when I'm updating an existing token, because in AssemblyScript that constructor gives you a totally blank entity — none of whatever was saved for that token before carries over automatically. So the pattern is always load first: `Token.load(id)`, check if it's null, and only construct a new one if it genuinely doesn't exist yet. If it does exist, I take that loaded entity, update just the owner field, and save it back — that's how I preserve anything else that's already stored on it, like metadata I might have set in a different handler. If I skipped the load and just constructed fresh every time, I'd be silently nuking any previously indexed data on that token on every single transfer event, and that bug wouldn't throw an error anywhere — it would just quietly corrupt my indexed data, which is exactly the kind of thing that's miserable to debug later.
commonMistakes: Always calling `new Entity(id)` instead of checking Entity.load(id) first, wiping prior field values
Using a non-unique ID (e.g. just tokenId) for an immutable per-event entity like Transfer
Forgetting to call .save() after mutating an entity, so changes are never persisted
Not handling the null case explicitly when Entity.load() returns null for a never-seen entity
Mixing up event.params (decoded event args) with event.block or event.transaction fields
keyPoints: Immutable per-event entities (Transfer) use a unique ID combining tx hash and log index
Stateful entities (Token) must be loaded via Entity.load(id) before mutation
A fresh `new Entity(id)` always produces blank fields, discarding previously saved data
Handling the null case from .load() distinguishes first-seen entities from existing ones
Every created or mutated entity must call .save() to persist to the subgraph store

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly decodes event.params into a new Transfer entity with a unique ID
Correctly loads the existing Token entity before mutating it
Correctly handles the null case for a first-seen entity
Explains why load-before-mutate is necessary in AssemblyScript mapping handlers

questions.title: Verifying a SIWE Signature Server-Side in Node.js
questions.prompt: Write server-side Node.js code (using viem or ethers) that takes a submitted SIWE message and signature, verifies the signature against the claimed address, checks the nonce against a server-stored value, and issues a session only if all checks pass. Explain what you check and in what order, and why order matters here.
questions.modelAnswer: The verification function must perform checks in a specific order because some checks are cheap and purely structural (and should fail fast before spending effort on cryptographic verification), while others depend on earlier checks having already extracted trustworthy data. First, parse the SIWE message and confirm it's well-formed and contains a nonce, domain, and expiration field in the expected format — reject malformed messages immediately. Second, check the expiration timestamp against the current server time and reject if expired, since there's no reason to cryptographically verify a message that's already stale. Third, check the domain field against the server's own expected domain, rejecting if it doesn't match, which prevents a signature collected for a phishing domain from being replayed against the legitimate backend. Fourth, perform the actual cryptographic verification: recover the signer's address from the signature over the exact message bytes and confirm it equals the claimed address — this must happen before trusting anything else about 'who signed this,' since nothing prior to this point has cryptographically proven the claimed address actually produced the signature. Fifth, only after the signature is confirmed valid, look up the nonce in server-side storage (keyed by the address or by a pending-login session id), confirm it matches exactly what was issued and has not already been marked consumed, then immediately mark it consumed (single-use) before issuing a session token — checking the nonce before signature verification would let an attacker probe which nonces are valid without ever proving key ownership, and failing to invalidate the nonce immediately after success would allow the exact same signed message to be replayed to create additional sessions.
questions.professionalAnswer: I always think about this as fail-fast-and-cheap-first, then-do-the-expensive-cryptographic-check, then-the-stateful-check-last. So first I parse the message and just sanity-check its shape — does it have a nonce, a domain, an expiration, is it even well-formed SIWE. If not, reject immediately, no point doing anything expensive. Then I check expiration against the current time, because again, that's free and if it's expired there's zero reason to go verify a signature on a stale message. Then — and this one's easy to forget — I check the domain field in the message against my own server's actual domain, because if I skip that, someone could get a user to sign a SIWE message for a phishing site and then try to replay that exact signed message against my real backend, and cryptographically it would look totally valid. Only after those cheap structural checks pass do I do the actual signature recovery — pull the signer's address back out of the signature and the exact message bytes, and compare it to the address the client claims to be. That has to happen before I trust anything about 'who is this,' because up to this point nothing has actually proven that. And the very last thing I check, deliberately last, is the nonce — I look it up server-side, confirm it matches what I issued and hasn't already been used, and the moment it passes I immediately mark it consumed in the same operation before I issue the session. I check the nonce last and not first specifically because if I checked it before verifying the signature, I'd be leaking information — someone could probe my server with garbage signatures just to figure out which nonces are currently valid. And invalidating it immediately on success, not after, is what stops the exact same signed message from being replayed a second time to spin up another session.
commonMistakes: Checking the nonce before verifying the signature, leaking which nonces are valid to unauthenticated probing
Forgetting to check the domain field, allowing a phishing-collected signature to be replayed
Not marking the nonce as consumed immediately, allowing the same signature to create multiple sessions
Verifying the signature against the message's claimed address without confirming that address matches the session request
Skipping expiration checks, allowing stale signed messages to remain valid indefinitely
keyPoints: Cheap structural checks (format, expiration, domain) run before expensive cryptographic verification
Signature verification recovers the signer and must match the claimed address before trusting it
Nonce validation happens after signature verification, not before, to avoid leaking valid nonces
The nonce must be marked consumed atomically with success to prevent replay
A session is issued only after every check passes, in the correct order

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly verifies the signature against the claimed address
Correctly checks and invalidates the nonce (single-use)
Checks domain and expiration fields appropriately
Explains and applies a defensible check ordering

questions.title: Reading a Chainlink Price Feed With a Staleness Check
questions.prompt: Write Solidity code that reads a price from a Chainlink `AggregatorV3Interface` feed and includes a staleness check that reverts if the price's `updatedAt` timestamp is older than an acceptable threshold. Explain why skipping the staleness check is dangerous even if the feed address itself is correct and trustworthy.
questions.modelAnswer: AggregatorV3Interface.latestRoundData() returns (roundId, answer, startedAt, updatedAt, answeredInRound). A correct consumer must check updatedAt against block.timestamp and revert if the difference exceeds an acceptable maximum staleness threshold, in addition to checking that answer is a sane positive value (Chainlink feeds can technically return 0 or negative values in edge/outage cases, which should also be rejected). Skipping the staleness check is dangerous even when the feed address itself is legitimate because Chainlink's update model is heartbeat/deviation-based, not continuous: a feed only pushes a new on-chain update when the price has moved past its deviation threshold or when the heartbeat interval elapses, and in practice the oracle node network, the underlying chain, or the data sources themselves can experience outages, congestion, or delisting events that cause updates to stop arriving entirely for an extended period. If a consuming contract blindly trusts the last reported value with no freshness check, during such an outage it keeps using a price that no longer reflects the real market — and because this is a trusted, 'legitimate' price feed, the failure mode isn't an obvious revert, it's a silent, confidently-wrong number that a lending protocol might use to value collateral or trigger liquidations incorrectly, a real failure mode that has caused losses in production DeFi protocols during feed outages.
questions.professionalAnswer: The basic call is `latestRoundData()`, which hands back roundId, the answer, startedAt, updatedAt, and answeredInRound. The part people skip is checking that `updatedAt` against `block.timestamp` — I always subtract the two, and if that gap is bigger than some threshold I've decided is acceptable for this specific feed, I revert right there rather than use the price. I'd also sanity check that answer is actually positive, because Chainlink feeds can technically report zero or negative in genuine outage edge cases, and a negative price silently flowing into downstream math is its own disaster. Now, why does this matter even when I trust the feed itself completely? Because Chainlink feeds aren't continuously streaming — they only push a new update when the price moves past a deviation threshold or a heartbeat timer fires, which is by design, to save gas. That means there can be real gaps between updates even in totally normal operation, and in an actual outage — node problems, chain congestion, whatever — those gaps can stretch a lot longer than expected. If my contract just calls latestRoundData and blindly uses whatever comes back with zero freshness check, during an outage I'm not getting an error, I'm getting a confident, old, wrong number, and depending on what I'm doing with it — valuing collateral, deciding whether to liquidate someone — that stale number can cause real financial damage without ever throwing a single revert to warn me something's wrong. That's exactly the kind of failure that's happened for real in production DeFi during feed outages, so I treat the staleness check as completely non-negotiable, not an optional hardening step.
commonMistakes: Calling latestRoundData() and using answer directly with no freshness or sanity check at all
Checking updatedAt but comparing it incorrectly (e.g. wrong direction of subtraction)
Not rejecting zero or negative answer values as potential outage/error signals
Assuming a trustworthy feed address guarantees the returned price is current
Picking an arbitrary staleness threshold without considering the specific feed's actual heartbeat interval
keyPoints: latestRoundData() returns updatedAt, which must be compared against block.timestamp
A maximum staleness threshold should be chosen relative to the feed's known heartbeat
answer should also be checked for sane (positive, nonzero) values
Chainlink feeds update on deviation/heartbeat triggers, not continuously, so gaps are normal but bounded
Trusting a legitimate feed address does not guarantee the most recent value is current during an outage

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly calls latestRoundData() and extracts updatedAt/answer
Correctly implements the staleness check against a threshold
Checks answer for sane/positive values
Explains why staleness matters even with a trustworthy feed address

questions.title: Managing Nonces for Concurrent Transactions From One Hot Wallet
questions.prompt: A backend service sends multiple transactions concurrently from a single hot wallet (e.g., processing several withdrawal requests at once). Write Node.js code that safely assigns sequential nonces to avoid 'nonce too low' or stuck-transaction collisions, and explain the race condition that occurs if each concurrent transaction simply calls `getTransactionCount()` independently right before sending.
questions.modelAnswer: If each concurrent transaction independently calls getTransactionCount() (or eth_getTransactionCount) immediately before sending, all of them race against the same on-chain state: since none of the concurrently-submitted transactions have been mined yet, getTransactionCount() returns the same 'next nonce' value to every caller that queries before any of them lands, causing multiple transactions to be assigned the identical nonce. Only one of those transactions can ultimately be accepted by the network (nonces must be used exactly once, in order); the others either get rejected outright as 'nonce too low'/duplicate once the first lands, or worse, silently replace (if gas price differs) or get stuck pending indefinitely if the node treats them as valid-but-unconfirmed replacements. The correct fix is to centralize nonce assignment in-process: maintain an in-memory counter, initialize it once from the chain's current transaction count (ideally using the 'pending' block tag to include any already-submitted-but-unconfirmed transactions), and have every transaction-sending code path acquire the next nonce from this single counter atomically (e.g., incrementing synchronously before any async network call, or using a mutex/queue) rather than re-querying the chain per transaction. The counter must also be reconciled if a transaction fails to actually broadcast (e.g., decrement or mark the nonce available again) to avoid permanently skipping a nonce and stalling every subsequent transaction behind the gap, since EVM nonces must be used strictly in sequence with no gaps.
questions.professionalAnswer: The bug here is a classic race condition: if every concurrent send calls getTransactionCount() right before sending, they're all asking the chain 'what's my next nonce' at basically the same moment, and since none of those pending transactions have actually landed yet, the chain answers the same number to all of them. So now I've got, say, five transactions that all think they're nonce 42. Only one of those can actually succeed — nonces have to be used once, in strict order — and the rest either get flat-out rejected as 'nonce too low,' or depending on timing and gas price, one might even replace another instead of landing separately, which is its own mess to debug. The fix I'd reach for is to stop asking the chain per-transaction and instead own the nonce counter myself, in process. I initialize it once — ideally against the 'pending' tag so I account for anything already in flight — and from then on, every single send grabs its nonce by incrementing that one shared counter synchronously, before any of the actual async send logic runs, so two concurrent calls can never grab the same value. I'd implement that increment as a genuinely atomic step — synchronous in JS terms, or behind a small queue/mutex if the logic around it isn't trivially synchronous — because if the increment itself has an await in the middle of it, I've just reintroduced the exact race I was trying to kill. And one thing I always build in: if a transaction fails to actually broadcast for some reason, I have to release that nonce back or the counter gets ahead of reality, and since nonces can't have gaps, every transaction after that point gets stuck waiting on a nonce that will never be filled.
commonMistakes: Calling getTransactionCount() independently right before each concurrent send
Initializing the nonce counter without the 'pending' block tag, missing already-in-flight transactions
Incrementing the shared counter non-atomically (e.g. after an await), reintroducing the race
Not reconciling the counter when a transaction fails to broadcast, permanently stalling later transactions
Assuming higher gas price alone resolves a nonce collision rather than causing unpredictable replacement behavior
keyPoints: Independent getTransactionCount() calls race against the same unconfirmed chain state
Centralizing nonce assignment in a single in-process counter avoids duplicate assignment
The counter must be incremented atomically relative to concurrent callers
Initialization should use the 'pending' tag to include already-submitted transactions
Failed-to-broadcast transactions must release their nonce to avoid gaps stalling later sends

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly identifies the race condition from independent getTransactionCount() calls
Implements a centralized, atomic nonce-assignment mechanism
Initializes nonce state using the pending transaction count
Addresses reconciliation when a send fails to broadcast

questions.title: Foundry Invariant Test: AMM Pool k Never Decreases
questions.prompt: Write a Foundry invariant test for a constant-product AMM pool that asserts the pool's `k` value (reserve0 * reserve1) never decreases across any sequence of swaps, except for legitimate increases from collected fees. Explain what handler functions you'd expose to the fuzzer and why checking this invariant after every call, not just at the end, matters.
questions.modelAnswer: The invariant test needs a Handler contract exposing bounded, realistic entry points the fuzzer can call in random order and with random arguments — typically swap0for1(uint256 amountIn), swap1for0(uint256 amountIn), addLiquidity(uint256 amount0, uint256 amount1), and removeLiquidity(uint256 lpAmount) — each wrapped with bound() calls to keep fuzzed amounts within realistic ranges (e.g., not zero, not larger than the caller's balance) so the fuzzer spends its budget on meaningful states rather than reverting trivially. The handler should also track a lastK variable, updated after every successful call, so the invariant function can compare the pool's current k against the last known value rather than only an initial baseline. The invariant_kNeverDecreases() function then asserts current k is greater than or equal to lastK (since fees should only ever grow k, never shrink it, assuming no bug), called automatically by Foundry after every single handler call in the randomized sequence, not just once at the end of a run. This matters because a bug that temporarily violates the invariant mid-sequence — for example, a swap that briefly leaves k lower before some other state update 'fixes' it, or a sequence where one specific call ordering triggers rounding-direction errors that a different ordering wouldn't — would be invisible if only checked at the very end, since the end-state might happen to still satisfy the invariant even though it was violated partway through. Checking after every call is what actually catches order-dependent and intermediate-state bugs, which is the entire point of invariant testing over simple end-to-end assertions.
questions.professionalAnswer: For the handler, I'd expose the realistic actions a real user could take against this pool — swap in each direction, add liquidity, remove liquidity — and I'd bound every fuzzed input so Foundry isn't wasting its run budget on degenerate cases like swapping zero or trying to remove more LP tokens than the actor actually holds. I'd also have the handler itself track the last known k value as a piece of ghost state, updated right after every successful call, because the invariant function needs something to compare against besides just the very first k at setup. Then the invariant function itself is simple: current k has to be greater than or equal to that last recorded k, because fees should only ever push k up, never down, if everything's working correctly. The thing I'd really stress in an interview is why Foundry checking this after every single call in the sequence matters, not just once at the end. If I only checked at the end, I could easily miss a bug that causes k to dip mid-sequence and then get papered back over by a later call — the end state looks fine, so a naive 'just assert once at the end' test passes clean, but there was a real violation hiding in the middle that a user could have exploited by stopping their interaction with the pool at exactly that point. Invariant testing's whole value proposition is catching exactly that kind of order-dependent, intermediate-state bug, and that only works if the property gets re-checked after every single randomized call, which is exactly what Foundry's invariant runner does by default.
commonMistakes: Exposing unbounded fuzzed inputs, wasting the fuzzer's budget on trivially reverting calls
Not tracking a running lastK, comparing only against an initial baseline instead
Assuming a single end-of-run assertion is equivalent to checking after every call
Forgetting to call targetContract() to register the handler with the fuzzer
Not accounting for legitimate fee-driven increases, causing false-positive invariant failures
keyPoints: Handler exposes bounded, realistic entry points (swap both directions, add/remove liquidity)
Fuzzed inputs should be bound() to avoid trivial reverts and wasted fuzzing budget
A running lastK value, updated per call, is needed for a meaningful comparison
The invariant is checked after every call in the random sequence, not just at the end
Checking after every call is what catches order-dependent/intermediate-state bugs

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Defines a reasonable handler with bounded swap/liquidity functions
Correctly implements the k-never-decreases invariant check
Tracks running state (lastK) rather than only an initial baseline
Explains why per-call checking (not just end-of-run) matters

questions.title: Foundry Fuzz Test: Vault Withdraw Cannot Exceed Balance
questions.prompt: Write a Foundry fuzz test for a vault contract's `withdraw(uint256 amount)` function that asserts a user can never successfully withdraw more than their own recorded balance, across arbitrary fuzzed withdrawal amounts. Explain how you'd set up the fuzzed scenario (depositing first) so the test is meaningful rather than trivially always reverting or always passing.
questions.modelAnswer: A meaningful fuzz test needs the setup itself to establish a realistic, varied starting state before the behavior under test runs, otherwise the fuzzer either always exercises the same trivial zero-balance case or the test degenerates into checking nothing useful. The test should take two fuzzed parameters, depositAmount and withdrawAmount, bound depositAmount to a reasonable nonzero range (e.g., 1 to some realistic max, avoiding overflow edge cases that aren't the point of this specific test), have the test user actually deposit that amount first (funding the user with that amount of the underlying token and approving/depositing into the vault), and then attempt to withdraw the fuzzed withdrawAmount. The assertion logic must branch on the relationship between the two fuzzed values: if withdrawAmount is less than or equal to the user's actual recorded balance (which should equal depositAmount if deposits are tracked correctly), the withdraw call should succeed and the user's balance should decrease by exactly withdrawAmount; if withdrawAmount exceeds the recorded balance, the call must revert, and the test should assert this revert happens (using vm.expectRevert() before the call) rather than letting an unexpected success pass silently. This structure, bound-deposit-then-fuzz-withdraw-with-branching-assertion, is what makes the test actually exercise the boundary condition across many random pairs of (depositAmount, withdrawAmount), including cases right at the equality boundary, rather than either always trivially succeeding on tiny amounts or always trivially reverting on absurdly large ones.
questions.professionalAnswer: The trap with a naive version of this test is that if I just fuzz withdrawAmount against an empty vault, every single run reverts for the same boring reason — insufficient balance — and I haven't actually tested the interesting case at all. So the setup has to fuzz the deposit too, not just the withdrawal: I bound depositAmount to something realistic and nonzero, actually have the user deposit that amount first, and only then fuzz the withdrawAmount on top of that real balance. Then the assertion has to branch, because there are genuinely two valid outcomes depending on how the two fuzzed numbers relate to each other. If withdrawAmount is less than or equal to what the user actually has — which should just be depositAmount if the vault's accounting is correct — the withdrawal needs to succeed and I check the user's balance dropped by exactly that amount. If withdrawAmount is bigger than the balance, I use vm.expectRevert() right before that call, because the correct, desired behavior here is a revert, and if it doesn't revert, that's the actual bug I'm trying to catch — someone pulling out more than they put in. The value of fuzzing both numbers together rather than hardcoding the deposit is that Foundry will naturally wander into edge cases I might not think to write by hand, like withdrawAmount exactly equal to depositAmount, or off by one in either direction, which is exactly where balance-tracking bugs tend to hide.
commonMistakes: Fuzzing only withdrawAmount against an empty/fixed vault, making every run trivially revert for the same reason
Not bounding depositAmount, risking unrelated overflow failures masking the real test intent
Missing the branching assertion, asserting only success or only revert instead of both valid outcomes
Forgetting vm.expectRevert() before the over-withdrawal attempt, letting an unexpected success pass silently
Not checking the exact post-withdrawal balance, only that the call didn't revert
keyPoints: Both deposit and withdraw amounts should be fuzzed to create varied, realistic starting states
Deposit amount is bound to a realistic nonzero range to avoid unrelated edge-case noise
Assertion branches: success + exact balance decrease when within balance, revert when over
vm.expectRevert() is used explicitly to assert the over-withdrawal path fails as intended
Fuzzing both values together naturally exercises boundary conditions like exact equality

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Fuzzes and bounds both deposit and withdrawal amounts meaningfully
Correctly sets up a real deposit before testing withdrawal behavior
Correctly implements the branching assertion for both valid outcomes
Explains why this setup avoids a trivially always-reverting or always-passing test

questions.title: GitHub Actions CI That Blocks Merges on Test or Slither Failure
questions.prompt: Write a GitHub Actions workflow YAML for a Foundry smart contract project that runs `forge test`, runs Slither static analysis, and is configured so that a pull request cannot be merged if either step fails. Explain what makes a CI job actually 'block' a merge versus just reporting a status.
questions.code:
name: ci
on:
  pull_request:
    branches: [main]

jobs:
  test:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      # TODO: install Foundry, forge test, Slither
questions.modelAnswer: A workflow that runs forge test and Slither on pull requests reports a check status back to GitHub for that commit, but that status reporting alone does not block merging — merging is blocked only when the repository's branch protection rules on the target branch (e.g., main) are configured to require that specific check (by its job/status name) to pass before the merge button becomes available, and that protection applies to everyone including repo admins unless an explicit bypass is configured. The workflow itself needs: a trigger on pull_request, a job that checks out the code, installs Foundry (via the official foundry-toolchain action), runs forge test (which exits non-zero on any failing test, which GitHub Actions interprets as job failure), and separately runs Slither (via its action or a pip install + slither . invocation), configured to fail the step on any finding at or above a chosen severity rather than only printing output and exiting zero regardless of findings — a common mistake is running Slither in a way that always exits 0, which produces a report but never actually fails CI. Both steps need to be in a job (or jobs) whose overall result becomes 'failure' if either step fails; by default, a step failing in GitHub Actions fails the entire job and workflow run unless continue-on-error is set (which would defeat the purpose here). It's the combination of (a) the workflow actually producing a failing status on real failures and (b) branch protection requiring that exact status check that creates an enforced block — either piece alone is insufficient.
questions.professionalAnswer: There are really two separate pieces that both have to be right, and people often only do one. The first piece is the workflow itself: it needs to check out the repo, install Foundry — I'd use the official foundry-toolchain action for that — run forge test, and separately run Slither, and critically, both of those have to actually propagate a nonzero exit code when something's wrong. That sounds obvious but it's a real gotcha with static analysis tools specifically — some Slither setups will happily print a report of findings and still exit 0, which means the step shows green in GitHub Actions no matter what it found, and nothing fails. So I'd make sure Slither's invocation is actually configured to exit nonzero on findings above whatever severity I care about. Same logic for forge test — that one's usually fine by default since a failing test naturally exits nonzero. The second piece, and this is the one people forget entirely, is that none of this blocks a merge by itself. A workflow running on a PR just reports a status check next to the commit — it's informational unless I go into the repo's branch protection settings for main and explicitly mark that status check as required. Once I do that, GitHub actually greys out the merge button until that check comes back green, and that applies to everyone, not just external contributors, unless someone's explicitly set up an admin bypass. So the honest answer to 'what makes this actually block a merge' is: branch protection rules requiring the specific named check, paired with a workflow that's actually wired to fail loudly instead of silently reporting.
questions.example:
name: ci
on:
  pull_request:
    branches: [main]
jobs:
  test:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - uses: foundry-rs/foundry-toolchain@v1
      - run: forge test -vvv
      - uses: crytic/slither-action@v0.4.0
        with:
          fail-on: high
Then, in Settings > Branches > main, 'Require status checks to pass before merging' must list this job's check name.
commonMistakes: Running Slither in a configuration that always exits 0 regardless of findings, silently passing CI
Assuming a passing/failing CI workflow alone blocks merges without configuring branch protection
Not requiring the specific check by name in branch protection settings
Using continue-on-error on a step that should actually fail the job on error
Forgetting that branch protection can be bypassed by admins unless explicitly restricted
keyPoints: forge test and Slither must be configured to exit nonzero on real failures
A workflow reporting status alone does not block merges by itself
Branch protection rules must explicitly require the named status check
continue-on-error or lenient tool flags can silently defeat the intended blocking behavior
Enforcement requires both a correctly-failing workflow and correctly-configured branch protection

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Workflow correctly runs forge test and Slither on pull requests
Configures both steps to fail the job on real failures/findings
Explains that branch protection, not the workflow alone, enforces the block
Notes the common Slither always-exits-0 pitfall

questions.title: Foundry Deployment Script Transferring Ownership to a Multisig
questions.prompt: Write a Foundry deployment script that deploys a contract and then transfers its ownership to a Gnosis Safe multisig address, rather than leaving the deployer's private key in control after launch. Explain the specific risk this protects against and why transferring ownership in the same script run (versus a later manual step) matters.
questions.modelAnswer: The specific risk being protected against is that the deployer's private key, held by a single individual (or a single CI secret), remains the sole holder of privileged control (owner/admin functions like pausing, upgrading, or parameter changes) over a production contract indefinitely if ownership transfer is left as a manual follow-up step — a single compromised key, a departed team member, or simple human error in forgetting to run the transfer at all leaves the entire protocol's privileged functionality exposed to one point of failure with no multi-party approval requirement. The deployment script should use Foundry's vm.startBroadcast()/vm.stopBroadcast() to send real transactions from the deployer key: first deploying the contract, then immediately calling transferOwnership(SAFE_ADDRESS) (or an equivalent two-step process like transferOwnership + the Safe separately calling acceptOwnership(), if the contract implements the safer two-step pattern to avoid transferring to an unreachable/incorrect address) within that same script execution, before the script exits. Performing this in the same script run rather than as a separate later manual transaction matters because it removes the window during which a freshly-deployed, fully-functional, privileged contract sits reachable on-chain with only the single deployer key in control — that window is exactly when an attacker monitoring new deployments or a compromised CI pipeline has the highest-value, least-defended target, and any gap between deployment and ownership transfer is pure unmitigated single-key risk with no operational justification for existing, since the transfer logic is deterministic and can simply be scripted to run immediately after deployment succeeds.
questions.professionalAnswer: The risk I'm closing here is pretty direct: the second a contract with owner-gated functions like pause or upgrade gets deployed, whoever controls that deployer private key has full privileged control over it, and if transferring that control to the multisig is a separate, manual, 'I'll do it later' step, there's a real window where a single key — one person, one CI secret — is the only thing standing between the protocol and anyone who compromises that key. People leave for other jobs, keys get phished, CI secrets leak — any of those during that gap and it's game over, no multisig threshold protecting anything yet. So my approach is to just never create that gap at all — the ownership transfer happens inside the exact same script run as the deployment, using Foundry's broadcast block, so by the time the script finishes executing, the deployed contract is deployed AND already pointed at the Safe, back to back, no manual step for anyone to forget or delay. If the contract supports a two-step ownership pattern — propose, then have the Safe accept — I'd use that instead of a one-shot transfer, because a typo'd address in a single-step transfer can permanently lock the contract with no owner at all, which is its own disaster; two-step means the Safe has to actively claim it, so a bad address just fails safely. But the core principle stands regardless of one-step or two-step: I don't want 'transfer ownership to the Safe' living as a separate ticket or a manual follow-up — I want it baked into the same deploy script so it's impossible to forget and the single-key exposure window is as close to zero as I can make it.

Using a one-step transferOwnership without considering a safer two-step propose/accept pattern
Hardcoding or mistyping the Safe address without verifying it on-chain before broadcasting
Leaving the deployer key with any residual privileged role after transfer (e.g. forgetting a second admin role)
Not treating the gap between deployment and ownership transfer as a real, exploitable attack window

Ownership transfer should execute in the same script run as deployment, not a later manual step
A two-step propose/accept ownership pattern avoids permanently locking a contract on a bad address
The deployment-to-transfer gap is a real, actively exploitable attack window if left open
All privileged roles, not just 'owner', should be checked and transferred as needed

questions.title: Implementing getAmountOut() With a 0.3% Fee
questions.prompt: Write the Solidity `getAmountOut()` function for a constant-product AMM that calculates swap output including a 0.3% trading fee taken from the input amount. Explain exactly where in the calculation the fee is applied and why applying it to the input rather than the output changes the math.
questions.modelAnswer: The standard approach taxes the input amount before it's used in the constant-product formula: amountInWithFee = amountIn * 997 (representing 99.7%, i.e., a 0.3% fee, using integer arithmetic scaled by 1000 to avoid floating point), and then the output is computed as amountOut = (amountInWithFee * reserveOut) / (reserveIn * 1000 + amountInWithFee), which is the standard derivation of dy = y*dx_effective / (x + dx_effective) scaled consistently by the 1000 factor introduced for the fee, where dx_effective is the fee-reduced input. Applying the fee to the input rather than the output matters mechanically because it changes what actually gets added to the pool's reserves: taxing the input means the full 0.3% fee amount effectively stays in the pool, permanently increasing reserveIn (and therefore k) by that fee portion once the swap completes, since only the fee-reduced amount is used in the calculation that determines amountOut, while the full, un-fee-reduced amountIn is what actually gets transferred into the pool's reserve. If the fee were instead taken off the output (computing the full-amount swap output then subtracting 0.3% from amountOut before sending it to the trader), the fee amount would need to be separately redirected back into the pool to similarly grow k and compensate LPs, and the two approaches produce subtly different numerical results and different edge-case behavior (e.g., different rounding, different behavior as amountIn or reserves approach extreme values), which is why protocols are precise about documenting which convention they use.
questions.professionalAnswer: The way I'd write this is to tax the input before it ever touches the constant-product formula. So amountIn times 997, which represents keeping 99.7% of it — that's my 0.3% fee baked in using integer math, no floating point. Then I plug that fee-reduced amount into the standard output formula, but I have to scale the denominator by 1000 to stay consistent with the 997 numerator, so it ends up looking like (amountInWithFee * reserveOut) divided by (reserveIn * 1000 plus amountInWithFee). The reason I apply the fee to the input side and not by just computing the full swap and then shaving 0.3% off the output afterward comes down to what actually happens to the reserves. If I tax the input, the trader still sends the full, untouched amountIn into the pool — the fee-reduced number only shows up inside the math that decides how much they get back out. That means the full input amount lands in reserveIn, but they only get credit for the discounted portion when computing their output, and the difference just... stays in the pool, permanently, growing k a little with every trade. That's exactly the mechanism that pays liquidity providers — fees aren't swept out to some treasury, they're left behind as extra reserve depth. If instead I computed the full no-fee output and then subtracted the fee from what the trader receives, I'd have to go write separate logic to actually route that skimmed amount back into the pool's reserves to get the same LP-compensation effect, and the rounding behaves slightly differently too. So taxing the input isn't just a stylistic choice — it's the simpler path to the same economic outcome, which is part of why it's the convention most constant-product AMMs settled on.
questions.example: A swap of 1000 units in, with reserveIn=50000 and reserveOut=100000: amountInWithFee = 1000*997 = 997000. amountOut = (997000*100000) / (50000*1000 + 997000) = 99,700,000,000 / 50,997,000 ≈ 1955. The full 1000 units (not 997) are added to reserveIn, so the 3-unit fee-equivalent permanently deepens the pool.
commonMistakes: Using floating-point fee math instead of integer scaling (e.g. *997/1000), risking precision/rounding bugs
Applying the fee to the output and forgetting to route the skimmed amount back into reserves
Forgetting to scale the denominator by 1000 to stay consistent with the 997 numerator
Crediting only the fee-reduced amount into reserveIn instead of the full amountIn
Not explaining why the fee mechanically grows k and compensates LPs over time
keyPoints: Fee is applied to amountIn before the constant-product output calculation (e.g. amountIn * 997 / 1000)
The denominator must be scaled consistently with the fee-adjusted numerator
The full, un-discounted amountIn is what actually enters the pool's reserve
This mechanism is what permanently grows k and compensates LPs via fees
Taxing output instead of input would require separately routing the skimmed fee back into reserves

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly implements the 0.3% fee using integer-safe scaling
Correctly applies the constant-product formula with the fee-adjusted input
Explains why the fee is applied to input rather than output
