questions.title: Writing a Health Factor / Liquidation-Eligibility Function
questions.prompt: Write a Solidity function that calculates whether a lending pool position is eligible for liquidation, given the position's collateral value, debt value, and the asset's liquidation threshold. Explain the difference between the liquidation threshold and the collateral factor used at borrow time, and why using the wrong one in this function would be a serious bug.
questions.modelAnswer: The liquidation-eligibility check computes an adjusted collateral value by applying the liquidation threshold (expressed in basis points, e.g., 8500 for 85%) to the raw collateral value, then compares that adjusted value against the outstanding debt value: the position is liquidatable when adjustedCollateral < debtValue, equivalently when the health factor (adjustedCollateral / debtValue) falls to or below 1. The liquidation threshold and the collateral factor (sometimes called the borrow LTV cap) are deliberately different, distinct parameters even though both are expressed as a percentage of collateral value: the collateral factor is the more conservative limit applied at borrow time, capping how much a user is initially allowed to borrow against their collateral (e.g., 80%), while the liquidation threshold is a slightly higher percentage (e.g., 85%) representing the point at which a position becomes unsafe enough to liquidate. This gap between the two (80% borrow cap vs. 85% liquidation threshold) is intentional headroom: it means a position that borrowed the maximum allowed at origination isn't instantly at the liquidation boundary, giving some buffer against normal price volatility before liquidation risk kicks in. Using the collateral factor instead of the liquidation threshold in this function would be a serious bug because it would make every maximally-borrowed position liquidatable the instant it's opened (since borrowing right up to the 80% collateral factor would immediately fail an '80% adjusted value vs. debt' check), falsely flagging healthy positions and triggering liquidations that shouldn't happen, destroying user trust and potentially draining user collateral to liquidators for positions that were never actually at risk.
questions.professionalAnswer: The function itself is straightforward once you have the right inputs: take the raw collateral value, multiply it by the liquidation threshold — something like 8500 basis points for 85% — divide by 10000, and that gives you the adjusted collateral value. If that adjusted value is less than the outstanding debt, the position's liquidatable; equivalently, if you divide adjusted collateral by debt and get something at or below 1, same answer, same condition. The part I'd want to make sure I get right in an interview is the distinction between two numbers that sound similar but are not interchangeable: collateral factor and liquidation threshold. Collateral factor is the borrow-time cap — it's how much you're initially allowed to borrow against your collateral, and it's deliberately conservative, say 80%. Liquidation threshold is a different, usually slightly higher number, say 85%, that represents the actual danger line — the point where the position is unsafe enough that it should get liquidated. That gap between 80 and 85 isn't an accident or rounding — it's intentional breathing room, so that someone who borrowed the absolute maximum allowed at origination isn't sitting right at the liquidation edge from day one; they've got some cushion before normal price movement would put them at risk. If I accidentally used the collateral factor instead of the liquidation threshold in this exact function, every single position that borrowed right up to its allowed maximum would come back as liquidatable the moment it opened, because 80% adjusted collateral against the max debt it was allowed to take out is exactly at the boundary, maybe even under it depending on rounding. That's a catastrophic bug in production — healthy, properly-collateralized users would get liquidated immediately, losing collateral to liquidators for no real risk reason, which would be both a financial disaster and a trust-destroying event for the protocol.
commonMistakes: Using the collateral factor (borrow-time cap) instead of the liquidation threshold in the eligibility check
Comparing raw collateral value to debt without applying any threshold adjustment at all
Getting the basis-points division wrong (e.g. dividing by 100 instead of 10000)
Using strict inequality where the protocol's spec requires inclusive (<=) at the boundary, or vice versa
Not explaining the intentional gap between collateral factor and liquidation threshold as a safety buffer
keyPoints: Health factor compares threshold-adjusted collateral value against outstanding debt
A position is liquidatable when adjusted collateral falls to or below debt value
Collateral factor (borrow cap) and liquidation threshold are distinct, intentionally different percentages
The gap between them provides a volatility buffer for positions borrowed at the maximum allowed
Using the wrong parameter causes maximally-borrowed, healthy positions to be falsely liquidatable

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly implements the threshold-adjusted collateral calculation
Correctly implements the liquidation comparison condition
Correctly distinguishes liquidation threshold from collateral factor
Explains the consequence of using the wrong parameter

questions.title: Implementing the Reward-Per-Token-Stored Staking Pattern
questions.prompt: Write a Solidity staking contract fragment implementing the 'reward-per-token-stored' pattern, where rewards accrue linearly per second and must be correctly tracked per staker even though stakers deposit and withdraw at different times. Explain why naively tracking 'reward per second per staker' directly, instead of this pattern, breaks when the total staked amount changes over time.
questions.modelAnswer: The naive approach of tracking 'how much reward has this staker earned per second since they staked' breaks because the pool's total staked amount — the denominator that determines each staker's SHARE of the fixed pool-wide reward rate — changes every time anyone deposits or withdraws, not just when the specific staker being calculated does. If staker A's accrual rate depends on totalStaked at calculation time, but totalStaked changed multiple times while A was staked (because other stakers B, C, D came and went), any formula trying to directly compute A's accrued reward needs to account for every one of those intervals with their different totalStaked values — effectively requiring an on-chain loop over history, which is gas-prohibitive and doesn't scale. The reward-per-token-stored pattern solves this by tracking a single global accumulator, rewardPerTokenStored, representing cumulative reward earned per unit of staked token since the contract's inception, updated incrementally every time total supply changes: rewardPerToken() computes rewardPerTokenStored + (timeElapsed * rewardRate * 1e18) / totalStaked, reflecting the accrual since the last update at the CURRENT totalStaked (not needing history, because the stored value already captured all prior periods at their respective totalStaked values). Each staker's earned() reward is then computed as their balance times the DIFFERENCE between the current rewardPerToken() and a per-user checkpoint (userRewardPerTokenPaid[account]) recorded the last time that specific staker's own stake changed or claimed, plus any previously-tracked unclaimed rewards — meaning each staker's calculation only needs their own balance and their own last checkpoint, not the entire history of total-supply changes, because the global accumulator already absorbed that complexity on behalf of everyone.
questions.professionalAnswer: The naive version — just tracking some kind of per-second reward rate directly against each staker's deposit time — falls apart because the thing that determines how big a slice of the fixed reward rate any one staker gets is their balance divided by the TOTAL staked, and that total keeps moving every time anyone else stakes or unstakes, not just when the person I'm calculating for does something. So if I'm trying to figure out how much staker A earned since they joined, and three other people staked and unstaked at different points in between, their share of the pool was different in each of those sub-intervals, and a naive approach would need to replay all of that history for every single reward calculation — which is a loop that grows with every stake/unstake event ever, and that's just not something you can do cheaply on-chain. The reward-per-token-stored pattern sidesteps this entirely by keeping one global running total — rewardPerTokenStored — that represents cumulative reward per unit of stake since the beginning of time, and it gets bumped forward every time the total staked amount is about to change, using whatever totalStaked was valid up to that point. So rewardPerToken() is just: take that stored accumulator, add on however much has accrued since the last update at the current totalStaked, and that's the up-to-date global number — no history replay needed, because the stored value already baked in everything before this moment. Then for any individual staker, I don't need their whole history either — I just need their current balance, the current global rewardPerToken(), and a snapshot of what that global number was the last time THEIR balance changed, called userRewardPerTokenPaid. Multiply their balance by the difference between now and their snapshot, add whatever was already sitting in their rewards bucket, and that's their earned total. The elegance here is that the hard part — absorbing everyone else's stake/unstake activity — lives entirely in that one shared accumulator, so each staker's own calculation stays flat-cost regardless of how many other people have come and gone.
commonMistakes: Tracking per-staker accrual directly against time elapsed, ignoring that totalStaked changes affect everyone's share
Forgetting to update rewardPerTokenStored and lastUpdateTime before totalStaked changes
Not handling totalStaked == 0 as a special case, causing division by zero
Forgetting to checkpoint userRewardPerTokenPaid when a specific staker's balance changes
Mixing up when to add to rewards[account] versus relying only on the live earned() calculation
keyPoints: A naive per-staker direct calculation breaks because totalStaked changes affect everyone's accrual rate
rewardPerTokenStored is a single global accumulator updated whenever totalStaked changes
rewardPerToken() adds elapsed-time accrual at the current totalStaked to the stored accumulator
Each staker's earned() uses only their own balance and their own last checkpoint, not global history
This pattern keeps per-staker reward calculation at constant gas cost regardless of other stakers' activity

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly implements rewardPerToken() with the time-elapsed accumulator update
Correctly implements earned() using balance and per-user checkpoint difference
Explains why naive per-staker tracking breaks when totalStaked changes
Handles the totalStaked == 0 edge case

questions.title: Enforcing Timelock Delay in a Governance execute() Function
questions.prompt: Write a Solidity `execute()` function for a simple governance contract that enforces a minimum timelock delay has passed since a proposal's queued timestamp before it can be executed, and prevents double-execution. Explain the specific check ordering needed to avoid both a too-early execution bug and a replay/double-execution bug.
questions.modelAnswer: The function must perform, in order: first, confirm the proposal exists and was actually queued (queuedAt != 0, or an explicit status check), to reject calls on nonexistent or never-queued proposal IDs; second, confirm it has not already been executed (!proposals[proposalId].executed), rejecting a second execution attempt before doing anything else state-changing; third, confirm block.timestamp >= queuedAt + TIMELOCK_DELAY, rejecting any attempt to execute before the mandatory delay has elapsed. Critically, the executed flag must be set to true BEFORE the external call to the target contract is made (proposals[proposalId].executed = true; followed by the low-level call), following the checks-effects-interactions pattern — if the flag were set after the external call, a malicious or reentrant target contract could call back into execute() for the same proposalId during that external call, and since executed would still read false at that point, the reentrant call would pass the double-execution check and execute the proposal's payload again (or more, recursively) before the first call's state update ever lands, a classic reentrancy-enabled double-execution exploit. The timelock-delay check and the already-executed check can be ordered relative to each other without security consequence since both are pure reads that must both pass regardless of order, but the executed-flag write must unconditionally occur before the external interaction, not after, which is the one ordering constraint that is not just stylistic but necessary for correctness under reentrancy.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd structure the checks as: does this proposal exist and was it actually queued, has it already been executed, and has the timelock delay actually elapsed — all as require statements, read-only, and any order among those three is fine since they're just reads that all have to pass. The part where ordering actually matters for security, not just style, is what happens around the external call itself. I mark the proposal as executed — flip that boolean to true — before I make the external call to the target contract, not after. If I did it the other way, set the flag after the call succeeds, I've opened a reentrancy hole: if the target contract I'm calling into is malicious, or even just happens to call back into my governance contract during that external call, it could call execute() again for the exact same proposal ID, and because I haven't flipped executed to true yet, that check still reads false, so the reentrant call sails right through and executes the payload a second time — or more, if it keeps reentering — before my original call ever gets the chance to mark it done. So the rule I follow religiously is checks-effects-interactions: do all my require checks, make my state changes — in this case, flipping executed to true — and only then make the actual external call. That ordering is the one thing here that isn't negotiable; the delay check versus the already-executed check can go in whichever order reads more naturally, but effects-before-interaction on that executed flag is what actually prevents the double-execution exploit.
commonMistakes: Setting the executed flag to true after the external call instead of before, enabling reentrant double-execution
Omitting the already-queued/exists check, allowing calls against uninitialized proposal IDs
Using block.number instead of block.timestamp for a time-based delay (or vice versa inconsistently)
Not reverting on a failed external call, silently marking a failed execution as successful
Allowing the delay check to be bypassed via an off-by-one in the comparison (> instead of >=, or vice versa)
keyPoints: Existence/queued check, already-executed check, and timelock-elapsed check are all required before execution
The executed flag must be set to true before the external call, not after (checks-effects-interactions)
Setting the flag after the call enables a reentrancy-based double-execution exploit
The external call's success should be checked and reverted on failure
Read-only checks among themselves can be ordered flexibly; the effects-before-interaction rule cannot

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly implements all required require() checks (queued, not executed, delay elapsed)
Correctly sets the executed flag before making the external call
Explains the reentrancy risk of ordering this incorrectly
Checks and reverts on external call failure

questions.title: Subgraph Indexer Stuck Far Behind Chain Head
questions.prompt: A subgraph deployed on The Graph has been running fine for months, but the team now notices its sync status is stuck far behind the chain head — the dashboard that queries it is showing stale, incomplete data even though the underlying chain is producing blocks normally and RPC access is healthy. Walk through your diagnosis and fix.
questions.modelAnswer: A healthy chain with a stalled subgraph points almost entirely at the indexing layer, not the chain itself, so I'd start at the subgraph's own health endpoint (the `_meta`/indexing-status query against the Graph Node) rather than guessing. That tells me the exact block the subgraph is stuck at and whether `indexingError` is set. If there's a non-fatal or fatal handler error, the most common cause is a mapping handler that throws or asserts on a specific event at that block — an array out-of-bounds, an unexpected null, a division assumption that held for months until one transaction violated it — and Graph Node either halts indexing there (fatal) or endlessly retries the same block (non-fatal without `nonFatalErrors` enabled), which looks exactly like 'stuck.' I'd pull the Graph Node logs around that block height to find the actual exception and the triggering event/transaction. If there's no handler error, the next suspect is the RPC endpoint the Graph Node itself uses for `eth_call`/trace calls during mapping execution — that's separate from the application's own RPC and can be rate-limited or unhealthy independently. Once I've isolated it to a bad handler, the fix is to patch the mapping logic to handle the edge case defensively, then redeploy a corrected subgraph version — using grafting from the last good block of the broken version avoids a full historical resync, which could otherwise take hours. I'd also add alerting on indexing status going forward so this doesn't require a user complaint to surface.
questions.professionalAnswer: First thing I do is stop looking at the chain and look at the subgraph itself — hit its own health/status endpoint and see exactly which block it thinks it's at and whether there's an indexing error flagged, because 'stuck' and 'crashed' look identical from the dashboard's point of view but they're different problems. If there's an error, that's almost always a mapping handler choking on something — some event came through with a value or shape the code never anticipated, like an array index that's normally safe but wasn't this one time, and now the indexer's either dead at that block or looping on it forever trying to retry. I'd grab the Graph Node logs right around that block to see the actual thrown error and go find the transaction that triggered it. If the status endpoint says no error at all and it's just slow, then I'm looking at the RPC the Graph Node uses internally for calls during indexing — that's a totally separate connection from whatever the app uses, easy to forget about, and it can be rate-limited while everything else looks fine. Once I know it's a bad handler, I fix the logic, and critically, I don't just redeploy and let it resync from block zero — I graft the new version onto the last healthy block of the old one so it picks up right where it died instead of re-indexing everything. And I'm adding a monitor on indexing status after this, because finding out from a dashboard complaint instead of an alert is the real failure here.
questions.example: The `_meta` query returns `{ hasIndexingErrors: true, block: { number: 18234501 } }` while the chain head is at 18240112 — Graph Node logs show the same block repeating every retry with 'Mapping aborted: panic: array index out of bounds' traced to a swap handler hitting a pool with zero prior liquidity events.
commonMistakes: Assuming a stuck subgraph means the chain or the public RPC is unhealthy, without checking the subgraph's own status endpoint first
Not distinguishing a fatal handler error (indexing halted) from a non-fatal retry loop (indexing stuck repeating the same block)
Redeploying a fixed subgraph from scratch and triggering a full historical resync instead of grafting from the last good block
Overlooking that Graph Node has its own RPC dependency for mapping calls, separate from the application's RPC provider
Fixing the immediate edge case without adding monitoring on indexing status, so the same class of failure goes unnoticed again
keyPoints: Query the subgraph's own health/indexing-status endpoint first to find the exact stuck block and whether an error is flagged
A mapping handler throwing on an unanticipated event shape is the most common root cause of a stall
Graph Node's own RPC dependency for mapping calls is separate from the app's RPC and can fail independently
Use grafting to resume from the last good block rather than forcing a full resync after the fix
Add ongoing alerting on indexing status rather than relying on downstream data staleness to surface the issue

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly starts diagnosis at the subgraph's own indexing status rather than the chain/RPC
Identifies a mapping handler error as the likely root cause and explains how to find it in logs
Distinguishes fatal vs non-fatal indexing errors and their different stuck behaviors
Proposes grafting to avoid a full resync when redeploying the fix
Recommends ongoing monitoring/alerting on indexing status

questions.title: Chain Reorg Causes a Transfer Event to Be Credited Twice
questions.prompt: Your backend runs an event-listener service that credits a user's off-chain balance whenever it sees a `Transfer` event to their deposit address. After a shallow chain reorg, a user reports their balance is double what they actually deposited. Walk through your diagnosis and fix.
questions.modelAnswer: A double-credit right after a reorg is a strong signal that the listener is processing logs without any notion of 'this block might not be final,' and without idempotency keyed to something stable. During a reorg, the original block containing the Transfer gets replaced; if the listener was subscribed via a provider that re-emits logs for the new canonical chain (or if it was polling `getLogs` over overlapping ranges before and after the reorg without tracking which specific log it already handled), the same logical transfer can be delivered to the application twice — once from the orphaned block, once from the replacement block that re-includes an equivalent transaction (or the same transaction re-mined). If credits were applied directly from each delivered log without checking whether that exact event had already been recorded, the balance gets bumped twice. The fix has two layers: first, enforce idempotency at the data layer — store a unique constraint on (transactionHash, logIndex) or on (blockHash, transactionHash, logIndex) and skip crediting if that key already exists, so even a duplicate delivery can't double-apply. Second, and more fundamentally, don't treat a deposit as final until it has some confirmation depth (e.g., 12+ blocks), and handle `removed: true` logs from WebSocket subscriptions by reversing any provisional credit tied to that log. I'd also reconcile by replaying from a known-safe block after detecting a reorg to true up any state that drifted.
questions.professionalAnswer: The second I hear 'double credit right after a reorg,' I'm thinking the listener has no concept of finality and no idempotency key — it's just trusting that every log it receives represents a brand-new, never-before-seen event. During a reorg, the chain swaps out a block, and depending on how the listener's getting events — polling overlapping ranges, or a WebSocket subscription that doesn't properly handle the 'removed' flag — the same transfer can show up twice: once from the block that got orphaned, once from the replacement. If the code just says 'saw a Transfer, credit the balance' with no check against what it's already processed, that's exactly how you get a double credit. So the fix is really two things. First, make crediting idempotent — put a unique constraint in the database on the transaction hash plus log index, so no matter how many times that same event gets delivered, it only ever applies once. That alone stops the bleeding. But the deeper fix is not trusting an event until it's actually got some confirmations behind it — I wouldn't finalize a deposit at zero or one confirmation, I'd wait something like twelve blocks, and if I am listening live via WebSocket, I need to actually handle the 'removed: true' message and roll back any provisional state tied to it, not just ignore it. After something like this happens, I'd also want to reconcile — replay events from the last block I'm confident was safe and true up any balances that drifted during the incident.
questions.example: DB audit shows two rows for what should be one deposit: same amount, transaction hashes differing only because the second transaction was re-mined in the replacement block, both inserted roughly 30 seconds apart — with no unique constraint on (txHash, logIndex) to have blocked the second insert.
commonMistakes: Crediting balances directly from received logs with no idempotency key to detect duplicate delivery
Treating an event as final at zero or one confirmation instead of waiting for confirmation depth
Ignoring the `removed: true` flag on WebSocket log notifications during a reorg
Not reconciling or replaying state after a detected reorg to correct any drift
Assuming a reorg is rare enough to not need idempotent processing logic at all
keyPoints: Double-crediting after a reorg indicates missing idempotency, not a one-off bug in the reorg itself
A unique constraint on (transactionHash, logIndex) prevents duplicate credits regardless of delivery duplication
Deposits should require a confirmation depth before being treated as final
WebSocket subscriptions must handle `removed: true` logs to reverse provisional state
Post-incident reconciliation/replay is needed to correct any balance drift that already occurred

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly diagnoses the root cause as missing idempotency in event processing
Proposes a concrete idempotency mechanism (unique key on tx hash/log index)
Recommends confirmation depth before treating a deposit as final
Addresses handling of `removed: true` logs for live subscriptions
Includes reconciliation/replay to correct already-drifted state

questions.title: WebSocket Event Subscription Goes Silent After Provider Failover
questions.prompt: Your backend subscribes to on-chain events over a WebSocket connection to an RPC provider. After the provider performs a brief reconnect/failover on their end, your subscription stops delivering new events entirely — no error is thrown, the connection object still looks 'open,' and nobody notices until a user complains hours later. Walk through your diagnosis and fix.
questions.modelAnswer: A silent stall with no thrown error is the classic signature of a subscription that survived a transport-level reconnect but never re-registered its `eth_subscribe` call against the new underlying connection. Providers often fail over by swapping the node serving a WebSocket behind the scenes, or the client library auto-reconnects the socket itself, but subscription IDs are tied to the specific node/connection instance that issued them — once that instance is gone, the old subscription ID is dead even though the new socket reports itself as open and healthy. If the client code only listens for a 'close' event to trigger resubscription, and the failover didn't trigger a visible close (or the reconnect happened fast enough that the app's reconnect handler itself didn't re-subscribe), events simply stop arriving with nothing to indicate why. Diagnosing this means comparing the timestamp of the last received event against the provider's own incident/status log or against actual chain head progression — if blocks are being produced but nothing is arriving, the subscription is dead, not the chain. The fix is to never trust 'connection open' as a proxy for 'subscription active': add an explicit heartbeat/watchdog that tracks time since the last event against the expected block interval, and force a full disconnect-and-resubscribe (not just checking socket state) if that watchdog trips. A polling-based fallback that periodically double-checks via `eth_getLogs` over the recent range adds resilience against this exact failure mode, and the gap should trigger an alert, not get caught by a user.
questions.professionalAnswer: This one's sneaky because there's no error to chase — the connection object says it's open, so nothing in the code thinks anything's wrong. What's actually happened is the provider swapped the node behind that WebSocket during their failover, and the subscription ID I registered belongs to the old node instance, not the new one — so the socket is alive, but the subscription underneath it is dead. If my reconnect logic only fires on an actual 'close' event, and the provider's failover was slick enough that I never saw a close, I've got a subscription that looks fine and delivers nothing, forever, until someone notices stale data. To confirm that's what happened, I'd check the last event timestamp against real chain progression — if blocks kept coming but my feed went quiet at some point, that's the smoking gun, and I'd line that timestamp up against the provider's status page for their failover window. The actual fix is to stop trusting 'socket is open' as proof that anything's working — I want a watchdog that tracks how long it's been since I last got an event and compares that against how often I should be getting one, and if that gap gets too big, I force a full teardown and resubscribe rather than hoping the existing connection heals itself. I'd also keep a lightweight polling fallback running in the background — periodically calling getLogs over the recent range as a sanity check — specifically so a dead subscription can't go unnoticed for hours again, and I'd wire the watchdog to page someone rather than wait for a customer ticket.
questions.example: Event log shows last delivered event at 14:02 UTC; chain explorer confirms blocks continued every ~12 seconds afterward; provider's status page shows a 'brief connection migration' logged at 14:02:30 UTC — the subscription never fired again despite the socket's `readyState` reporting OPEN throughout.
commonMistakes: Treating a WebSocket connection's 'open' state as proof the subscription is still active
Only triggering resubscription on an explicit 'close' event, which a fast provider-side failover may not emit
Having no heartbeat/watchdog comparing time-since-last-event against expected block cadence
Relying solely on push-based subscriptions with no polling fallback as a sanity check
No alerting tied to subscription staleness, so the gap is discovered via a user complaint
keyPoints: A subscription ID is tied to a specific node instance and can go stale even if the socket reports open
Provider-side failovers can swap nodes without emitting a client-visible close event
A time-since-last-event watchdog, not socket state, is the correct liveness signal
A periodic polling fallback (e.g., getLogs) provides resilience against silent subscription death
Staleness should trigger proactive alerting rather than being discovered downstream

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly identifies that subscription IDs can die independently of socket connection state
Explains why reconnect-on-close logic alone misses this failure mode
Proposes a time-based watchdog as the correct liveness check
Recommends a polling fallback for resilience
Recommends proactive alerting on staleness

questions.title: RPC Rate Limiting Drops Transaction Submissions During a Traffic Spike
questions.prompt: During a sudden traffic spike, your backend starts receiving HTTP 429 responses from its RPC provider. Some user transaction submissions are silently delayed and others appear to be dropped entirely. Walk through your diagnosis and fix.
questions.modelAnswer: 429s mean the provider's rate limit for the current plan/key has been exceeded, so the first thing to establish is what's actually consuming the quota — is it genuine growth in legitimate user-initiated calls, or is some part of the backend making far more calls than necessary per user action (e.g., polling transaction status too aggressively, fetching full receipts in a loop, or re-fetching the same data per request instead of caching it)? I'd pull the provider's dashboard for request volume broken down by method to see if a few call types are disproportionately responsible. Independent of the root cause of volume, the deeper issue is that the system has no backpressure handling: a 429 should never result in a transaction submission being silently dropped — that implies there's no retry logic, or retries are failing without being surfaced or queued. The fix has several layers: add exponential backoff with jitter for retryable RPC errors so transient spikes don't cascade into dropped requests; batch read calls where possible instead of issuing them one at a time; cache data that doesn't need to be fetched fresh on every call; and queue transaction submissions through a durable queue rather than firing them synchronously inline with the user's request, so a provider hiccup delays rather than loses them. Longer-term, I'd add a secondary RPC provider and route around whichever one is currently rate-limiting, rather than depending on a single provider's capacity during spikes.
questions.professionalAnswer: 429 just means I've blown through the request quota on my current plan or key, so step one is figuring out what's actually eating that quota — is this just real spike-driven growth in users submitting transactions, or is some piece of the backend being wasteful, like polling for transaction status way more often than it needs to, or re-fetching the same chain data on every request instead of caching it. I'd go look at the provider's own usage dashboard broken out by RPC method, because that usually points straight at the offender. But honestly, the bigger problem here isn't the 429 itself, it's that a transaction submission can get silently dropped because of one — that tells me there's no retry logic, or the retry is failing quietly with nothing catching it. So the real fix stack is: exponential backoff with jitter on anything retryable so a burst of 429s doesn't just compound into more 429s; batching read calls instead of firing them one-by-one; caching anything that doesn't need to be dead-fresh every single time; and critically, putting transaction submissions behind a durable queue instead of firing them synchronously in the request path, so if the provider's having a bad minute, the user's transaction gets delayed and retried instead of just vanishing. And longer term, I don't want to be single-provider for something this load-sensitive — I'd want a second provider in the mix so I can fail over and route around whichever one is currently throttling me during a spike.
questions.example: Provider dashboard shows `eth_getTransactionReceipt` accounting for 70% of request volume during the spike, traced to a frontend polling loop hitting the backend every 500ms per pending transaction with no backoff — compounding rather than easing as 429s started.
commonMistakes: Not identifying which RPC methods are actually driving the volume before applying a generic fix
Having no retry/backoff logic, so a transient 429 results in a permanently dropped request
Submitting transactions synchronously inline with the user request instead of through a durable queue
Relying on a single RPC provider with no failover for load-sensitive operations
Polling for status aggressively instead of using subscriptions or caching to reduce call volume
keyPoints: Diagnose actual request volume by method before assuming the spike alone is the cause
429s should trigger exponential backoff with jitter, never a silent drop
Transaction submissions belong in a durable queue, not fired synchronously in the request path
Batching and caching reduce unnecessary RPC call volume
A secondary provider with failover reduces single-provider capacity risk during spikes

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly diagnoses what is driving RPC call volume rather than treating the spike as unavoidable
Identifies the lack of retry/backoff as the reason requests are dropped rather than delayed
Proposes a durable queue for transaction submission instead of synchronous inline calls
Proposes batching/caching to reduce unnecessary call volume
Recommends multi-provider failover as a structural fix

questions.title: Liquidation Executed Against a Stale Chainlink Price Feed
questions.prompt: A lending protocol integration reads a Chainlink price feed and uses `latestRoundData()` to value collateral. The feed hasn't actually updated in several hours — it's technically returning a valid-looking number, just an old one — and the protocol executes a liquidation against a user based on that stale price just before the real market price would have made the position healthy again. Walk through your diagnosis and fix.
questions.modelAnswer: `latestRoundData()` will happily return a syntactically valid answer even if the underlying feed hasn't updated recently — Chainlink feeds only push a new round when price moves beyond a deviation threshold or a heartbeat interval elapses, and under certain market or network conditions (e.g., low volatility combined with node issues, or the specific feed being thinly serviced) that heartbeat can be missed, leaving `updatedAt` far in the past while the contract has no built-in way of knowing that without checking. The root cause here is almost certainly that the integration consumed the `answer` field directly without validating `updatedAt` against a staleness threshold, and without checking `answeredInRound` against the current `roundId` to detect a carried-forward round. The immediate diagnosis is to pull the exact round data at the time of liquidation and compute `block.timestamp - updatedAt`; if that gap exceeds the feed's documented heartbeat, staleness is confirmed as the cause. The fix is to add an explicit staleness check that reverts (or routes to a fallback oracle/pause state) whenever that gap is too large, rather than trusting any value Chainlink returns unconditionally. Beyond the code fix, this incident needs an operational response: review whether the specific liquidation can be contested or compensated given it was based on bad data, and add monitoring/alerting on feed staleness so a live gap is caught before it causes another bad liquidation, not after.
questions.professionalAnswer: The trap here is that `latestRoundData()` doesn't fail or revert just because the feed is stale — it hands back a perfectly well-formed number, it's just an old one, and if nothing downstream checks the timestamp, the contract has no idea it's looking at hours-old data. Chainlink feeds only push an update when price moves past a deviation threshold or the heartbeat timer runs out, and there are conditions where that heartbeat gets missed, so the staleness itself isn't even that exotic — it's a known failure mode the integration just didn't guard against. So my diagnosis is straightforward: pull the round data from right before the liquidation, look at `updatedAt`, and compare that gap against what the feed's heartbeat is supposed to be. If that gap is way bigger than it should be, that confirms it — the code took the `answer` field at face value and never checked `updatedAt` or compared `answeredInRound` against the current round to catch a carried-forward value. The fix is to never consume a Chainlink price without that staleness check — if the gap's too big, revert the action or fall back to a secondary oracle rather than letting a liquidation happen on data that's effectively frozen. And separate from the code fix, this specific user got liquidated on bad information, so there's a real question of whether that liquidation gets reviewed or made whole — that's not just an engineering decision, but engineering needs to flag it. Going forward I'd also want active monitoring on feed staleness so this surfaces as an alert before it causes a liquidation, not after.
questions.example: At the time of liquidation, `updatedAt` reads a timestamp 5 hours and 40 minutes earlier against a feed with a documented 1-hour heartbeat and 0.5% deviation threshold — the price itself hadn't moved enough to trigger an update, but the heartbeat should have forced one and didn't, and nothing in the integration checked the gap before acting on the value.
commonMistakes: Consuming `latestRoundData()`'s answer directly without checking `updatedAt` against a staleness threshold
Assuming a feed returning a value at all means the value is current
Not checking `answeredInRound` against the current `roundId` to detect a carried-forward stale round
Having no fallback oracle or pause behavior when a staleness check would fail
Treating the fix as purely a code patch without addressing the already-executed bad liquidation
keyPoints: Chainlink feeds can return a valid-looking but stale value if the heartbeat is missed
A staleness check comparing `block.timestamp - updatedAt` against the feed's heartbeat is required before trusting a price
`answeredInRound` vs current `roundId` is a secondary signal for a carried-forward stale round
A failed staleness check should revert or fall back to a secondary oracle, not proceed
The already-executed bad liquidation needs an operational review, not just a code fix

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly explains why Chainlink can return a valid-looking but stale value
Identifies the missing staleness check (updatedAt vs heartbeat) as the root cause
Proposes a concrete fix: revert or fallback oracle on stale data
Addresses the operational/remediation angle for the bad liquidation, not just the code
Mentions ongoing monitoring/alerting on feed staleness

questions.title: Sign-In With Ethereum Users See Another User's Session Data
questions.prompt: Multiple users of a Sign-In With Ethereum (SIWE) dApp report an alarming bug: after logging in, they occasionally see another user's account data or an action performed under another user's session. Walk through your diagnosis and fix.
questions.modelAnswer: Users seeing each other's data under their own session is a session-isolation failure, not a signature-verification failure — the SIWE signature check itself can be perfectly correct while the session layer built on top of it leaks across users. The first thing I'd check is how sessions are created after a successful SIWE verification: if the session store keys sessions by something non-unique or predictable under concurrency (e.g., a shared in-memory object keyed by IP, a counter that can collide, or a session ID that isn't cryptographically random), two near-simultaneous logins can end up reading or writing the same session record. A second common cause is caching: if an API response for personalized data gets cached (by a CDN, a reverse proxy, or an in-process cache) without varying the cache key by session/user identity, one user's response can be served to the next request that hits the same cache key. A third candidate specific to SIWE is nonce handling — if the nonce isn't strictly single-use and tied to the specific address that requested it, a replayed or shared nonce could let one session's verification bleed into another's. Diagnosis means reproducing with two concurrent logins in a race and inspecting exactly what the session store and cache layer do under that race. The fix is to use cryptographically random, uniquely bound session identifiers, regenerate the session on every successful SIWE verification (preventing fixation), bind the session strictly to the verified address, enforce single-use nonces tied to the requesting address, and ensure personalized endpoints are never cached without a session-scoped cache key.
questions.professionalAnswer: This smells like a session isolation bug sitting on top of an otherwise-fine SIWE check — the signature verification can be totally correct and you can still get this if the session layer underneath it mixes people up. So I'd start by asking how a session actually gets created once someone's signature checks out: is the session ID truly random and unique, or is there some shared state — an in-memory store keyed off something that can collide, like IP address, or a predictable counter — where two people logging in around the same time could end up sharing a record. Caching is my second suspect, and honestly a very common one: if a personalized API response ever got cached by a CDN or a proxy or even an in-process cache without the cache key including who's asking, you can absolutely serve user A's data to user B just because they hit the same cached endpoint. Third, since this is SIWE specifically, I'd check the nonce — is it single-use and locked to the address that requested it, or could a nonce get reused or shared in a way that mixes up verification between two logins. To actually confirm which one it is, I'd try to reproduce it deliberately — fire two logins at nearly the same time and watch what the session store and any caching layer do under that race. The fix, regardless of which exact mechanism it turns out to be, is the same family of things: cryptographically random session IDs, regenerate the session fresh on every successful verification so there's no fixation, bind the session hard to the verified address, make nonces strictly single-use per address, and make sure anything personalized is never cacheable without the session baked into the cache key.
questions.example: Load test firing two SIWE logins within 15ms of each other shows both sessions landing in the same in-memory map slot because the session ID was derived from `Date.now()` truncated to the second — the second login's session object overwrote the first's reference held by the first user's browser.
commonMistakes: Assuming a correct SIWE signature check means the whole auth flow is secure, ignoring the session layer built on top
Using predictable or non-unique session identifiers that can collide under concurrent logins
Caching personalized API responses without varying the cache key by session or user identity
Not enforcing that a SIWE nonce is single-use and bound to the specific requesting address
Not regenerating the session on every successful login, leaving room for session fixation
keyPoints: Session isolation is a separate concern from SIWE signature verification correctness
Session identifiers must be cryptographically random and not derived from predictable/colliding inputs
Caching layers must vary by session/user identity for any personalized endpoint
Nonces must be single-use and bound to the specific address that requested them
Reproducing with concurrent logins is the most direct way to confirm a session-isolation race

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly separates session-layer bugs from SIWE signature verification correctness
Identifies session ID collision/predictability as a plausible root cause
Identifies cache-key-without-user-scoping as a plausible root cause
Identifies nonce reuse/sharing as a plausible root cause
Proposes a reproduction method (concurrent logins) and concrete session-hardening fixes

questions.title: Large AMM Swap Gets a Much Worse Price and the User Claims Being Sandwiched
questions.prompt: A user executes a large swap on your AMM-based DEX and ends up with a much worse execution price than the frontend's quoted estimate. They also claim they were 'sandwiched.' Walk through your diagnosis and how you'd respond to both the price discrepancy and the sandwich claim.
questions.modelAnswer: These are two related but distinct phenomena that need to be diagnosed separately. First, price impact: on a constant-product AMM, a large swap relative to pool depth moves the price along the curve by design — the quoted estimate from the frontend is typically computed at the moment of quoting, against the pool's reserves at that instant, but if the pool is shallow relative to trade size, the actual execution price after the trade's own impact can differ substantially from that quote even with zero adversarial behavior. I'd check the pool's reserve depth versus trade size to quantify how much of the gap is pure, expected price impact. Second, and separately, I'd check the block explorer for the transactions immediately before and after the user's in the same block: a classic sandwich shows a front-running buy from the same address (or a related address) immediately before the user's swap, and a back-running sell immediately after, both profiting from the price movement the user's trade caused. If that pattern is present, the user's transaction was visible in the public mempool and got targeted, independent of the AMM's own correctness. The response has two parts: for price impact, the frontend should better communicate realistic impact for the trade size (and potentially route through an aggregator or split the trade across pools/pathways to reduce impact), with slippage tolerance set to match, not just blindly widened. For the sandwich specifically, the structural fix is to stop broadcasting swaps to the public mempool — routing through a private transaction relay (e.g., Flashbots Protect or an MEV-aware RPC) prevents searchers from seeing and acting on the pending transaction before it lands.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd pull these two complaints apart because they're not actually the same problem even though they both show up as 'I got a bad price.' First, pure price impact: on a constant-product curve, a trade that's big relative to the pool just moves the price — that's not a bug, that's the AMM working as designed, and the frontend's quote was a snapshot taken a moment before, so if the pool's shallow for a trade this size, a real gap between quote and execution is expected with zero foul play. I'd check pool depth against the trade size first to see how much of this is just that. Separately, I'd go look at the block the user's swap landed in and check what happened immediately before and after it — a sandwich has a very distinctive signature: a buy right before from some address, the user's trade in the middle, a sell right after from that same or a related address, both legs profiting off the price move the user's own trade caused. If I see that pattern, the user's right, and it happened because their transaction sat visible in the public mempool where a bot could see it coming and react before it landed. So the response really has two tracks. On price impact, I'd improve how the frontend communicates realistic impact for a trade this size — maybe route it through an aggregator or split it across pools instead of hitting one pool all at once, and set slippage tolerance to match the real impact rather than just cranking it wider to make the error go away. On the sandwich side, the actual fix isn't anything inside the AMM contract itself — it's getting this transaction out of the public mempool entirely by routing through a private relay like Flashbots Protect, so the searcher bots never get a look at it before it's already final.
questions.example: Block explorer shows three transactions in the same block: a buy of 50,000 USDC worth of TOKEN from address 0xABC... at position 14, the user's 500,000 USDC swap at position 15, and a sell of the same TOKEN amount back from 0xABC... at position 16 — netting roughly 1.8% profit on the round trip, confirming a classic sandwich.
commonMistakes: Treating all of the price discrepancy as an attack without first quantifying expected price impact from pool depth versus trade size
Treating all of the price discrepancy as pure price impact without checking the block for an actual sandwich pattern
Responding to slippage complaints by simply widening slippage tolerance instead of addressing impact or routing
Assuming a sandwich can be fixed inside the AMM contract itself rather than at the transaction-routing/mempool-visibility layer
Not considering splitting large trades across pools or routing through an aggregator to reduce impact
keyPoints: Price impact from trade size relative to pool depth is expected AMM behavior, separate from any attack
A sandwich is confirmed by inspecting adjacent transactions in the same block for a front-run/back-run pattern from a related address
Price impact is best addressed via better frontend communication, routing, or splitting trades, not just wider slippage
Sandwich protection is achieved by avoiding public mempool exposure (private relay/MEV-aware RPC), not by AMM contract changes
The two issues require separate diagnosis even though they present as the same user complaint

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly separates price impact from sandwich attack as distinct phenomena
Explains price impact in terms of pool depth versus trade size on a constant-product curve
Describes how to confirm a sandwich by inspecting adjacent block transactions
Proposes appropriate responses to price impact (routing, splitting, slippage tuning)
Proposes the correct structural fix for sandwiching (private relay/mempool protection)

questions.title: Flash Loan Price Manipulation Drains a Lending Protocol
questions.prompt: Your lending protocol just lost a significant amount of funds. On-chain analysis shows the attacker took out a flash loan, used part of it to briefly skew a price source, then borrowed against collateral that was valued using that skewed price, and repaid the flash loan — all within a single transaction. Walk through your diagnosis of the attack mechanics and how you'd fix the protocol.
questions.modelAnswer: This is the canonical flash-loan price-manipulation pattern, and the root vulnerability is almost always that the protocol priced collateral using a source that can be moved within a single transaction — most commonly the spot reserve ratio of a single AMM pool — rather than a source that's resistant to single-block manipulation. Tracing the attack transaction confirms the mechanics: (1) flash-borrow a large amount of an asset with no collateral required since it's repaid in the same transaction, (2) use a portion of it to execute a large swap against the specific pool the lending protocol reads its price from, skewing that pool's reserve ratio far from the true market price, (3) deposit collateral and borrow against the now-inflated or deflated valuation while the price is still skewed, (4) reverse the swap (or simply let the flash loan's repayment step complete) and repay the flash loan, all atomically, walking away with the borrowed assets as profit since the collateral was never actually worth what the protocol believed. The fix is to decouple the price used for collateral valuation from anything manipulable within one transaction: switch to a time-weighted average price (TWAP) that can't be moved meaningfully in a single block, or to an external oracle like Chainlink that aggregates off-chain data and isn't subject to on-chain liquidity manipulation. Beyond the oracle fix, I'd add sanity bounds that reject or flag price deviations beyond a reasonable threshold within a short window, and consider disallowing deposit-and-borrow against newly-skewed collateral within the same block as a defense-in-depth measure. The incident itself requires pausing the affected market immediately and a full audit of every other price-dependent function in the protocol for the same class of vulnerability.
questions.professionalAnswer: Once I see 'flash loan, then a swap, then borrow, then repay, all in one transaction,' I already know roughly what happened — this is the textbook attack, and it only works because the protocol trusted a price that can be moved within a single transaction, which almost always means it was reading spot reserves off one AMM pool directly instead of something manipulation-resistant. Walking the attacker's transaction confirms it: they flash-borrow a big chunk of some asset — no collateral needed because it all gets repaid before the transaction ends — use part of that to slam a swap through the exact pool the lending protocol is reading its price from, which skews that pool's ratio way off real market price, then while it's still skewed they deposit and borrow against collateral that's now mispriced in their favor, then unwind the swap and pay back the flash loan, and the whole thing nets out atomically with them walking away with assets the protocol never should have lent out. The fix is about decoupling the price source from anything that can move in one block — that means TWAP pricing instead of instantaneous spot reserves, or pulling from an external oracle like Chainlink that isn't sourced from on-chain liquidity that an attacker can just push around with enough capital. I'd also want sanity-check bounds on top of that — if a price moves further than it reasonably should in a short window, the protocol should flag or reject it rather than act on it, as a second layer in case the primary oracle gets compromised too. And immediately, separate from the long-term fix, the affected market needs to be paused and every other function in the protocol that reads a price needs the same audit, because if one spot was vulnerable to this, there's a good chance it's not the only one.
questions.example: Transaction trace: flash-borrow 50M USDC → swap 20M USDC into a thinly-liquid collateral token on the one pool the protocol reads for pricing (reserves move from a 1:1 ratio to roughly 1:1.8) → deposit the now-overpriced collateral token and borrow against it at the inflated valuation → swap back → repay flash loan, all in one atomic transaction, netting the attacker the difference between true and manipulated collateral value.
commonMistakes: Pricing collateral from a single AMM pool's spot reserves instead of a TWAP or external oracle
Assuming flash loans themselves are the vulnerability rather than the manipulable price source they're used to exploit
Fixing only the specific pool/asset involved without auditing every other price-dependent function for the same pattern
Not adding sanity-bound checks on price deviation as a defense-in-depth layer beyond the primary oracle fix
Treating the incident as resolved without pausing the affected market immediately upon discovery
keyPoints: The attack's three-step mechanics: skew a manipulable price source, exploit it for an over/under-valued action, unwind atomically within one transaction
The root vulnerability is a price source manipulable within a single block, not the flash loan mechanism itself
TWAP pricing or an external oracle (e.g., Chainlink) decouples valuation from single-transaction manipulation
Sanity bounds on price deviation add defense-in-depth beyond the primary oracle fix
Immediate incident response requires pausing the affected market and auditing all other price-dependent functions

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly explains the full attack mechanics (flash loan, price skew, exploit, atomic unwind)
Identifies the manipulable spot price source as the true root cause, not the flash loan itself
Proposes TWAP or external oracle as the structural fix
Proposes sanity-bound checks as defense-in-depth
Addresses immediate incident response (pause, broader audit)

questions.title: Liquidations Fall Behind During a Market Crash and Bad Debt Accumulates
questions.prompt: During a sharp, fast market crash, a large number of undercollateralized positions on your lending protocol are not getting liquidated quickly enough. Bad debt starts accumulating on the protocol's balance sheet. Walk through your diagnosis and fix.
questions.modelAnswer: Liquidations lagging specifically during a crash points to the liquidation mechanism breaking down exactly when it's needed most, and there are a few independent contributors I'd check in parallel rather than assuming one cause. First, gas prices during a crash typically spike sharply as everyone rushes to react, and if the liquidation bonus/incentive isn't large enough relative to that spiked gas cost, liquidator bots become unprofitable to run and simply stop firing — I'd compare realized gas costs during the window against the liquidation bonus economics. Second, oracle latency: if the price feed's heartbeat or deviation threshold is too slow for how fast the market is actually moving, positions may not even show as undercollateralized on-chain until well after they actually are off-chain, delaying the trigger for liquidation entirely. Third, I'd check whether liquidation calls were being submitted but reverting — common causes include the liquidation pulling a stale price failing a staleness check (ironically a safety feature backfiring under load), or insufficient on-chain liquidity to actually execute the liquidation's swap step without excessive slippage. The fix needs to address each contributor: make liquidation incentives dynamic so they scale with gas conditions rather than being fixed; ensure the oracle's deviation threshold is tight enough to track genuinely fast-moving markets; make the liquidation function itself permissionless and gas-efficient so any bot can call it without protocol-specific friction; and consider a backstop mechanism (insurance fund or safety module) to absorb bad debt that does occur despite these measures, since under truly extreme conditions some bad debt may be unavoidable.
questions.professionalAnswer: When liquidations specifically fall behind during a crash, that's not bad luck, that's the liquidation system's economics or inputs breaking down right when load is highest — so I'm checking a few things in parallel rather than assuming it's just one thing. First, gas: crashes spike gas prices because everyone's reacting at once, and if the liquidation bonus doesn't scale with that, running a liquidation bot stops being profitable and they just stop firing — I'd pull gas costs during the window and check them against what the bonus actually pays out. Second, I'm checking the oracle's responsiveness — if the price feed's deviation threshold or heartbeat is too loose for how fast this crash is actually moving, positions might not even register as undercollateralized on-chain until the real damage is already way past what the protocol can see, so the liquidation trigger itself is late. Third, I want to know if liquidation calls were actually being attempted and reverting — maybe a staleness check meant to protect against bad oracle data is backfiring and blocking legitimate liquidations under load, or there just isn't enough on-chain liquidity to execute the liquidation's swap without it failing from slippage. Whichever combination of those it turns out to be, the fix touches all of them: liquidation incentives need to flex with gas conditions instead of being a fixed number, the oracle needs to be tight enough to track genuinely fast markets, the liquidation function itself needs to be permissionless and cheap enough that any bot can call it without friction, and on top of all that, I'd want some kind of backstop — an insurance fund or safety module — because under a truly extreme crash, some amount of bad debt might just not be preventable no matter how well-tuned everything is, and the protocol needs a way to absorb that without becoming insolvent.
questions.example: During the crash window, median gas price hit 450 gwei while the liquidation bonus (5% of a typical $2,000 position) netted roughly $100 — against a liquidation transaction costing upwards of $80 in gas alone, collapsing the profitable margin and causing most bots to stop submitting liquidations for smaller positions entirely.
commonMistakes: Assuming bad debt during a crash is simply unavoidable without checking whether liquidation incentives kept pace with gas costs
Not checking whether the oracle's deviation threshold/heartbeat was fast enough to flag undercollateralization in time
Not checking whether liquidation calls were reverting (stale price checks, insufficient swap liquidity) rather than simply not being attempted
Having a fixed liquidation bonus that doesn't scale with network conditions
No backstop/insurance mechanism to absorb bad debt that occurs despite a well-tuned liquidation system
keyPoints: Gas cost spikes during a crash can make liquidation unprofitable if the bonus doesn't scale accordingly
Oracle responsiveness (deviation threshold/heartbeat) determines how quickly undercollateralization is even detected
Reverting liquidation calls (stale price checks, insufficient swap liquidity) can silently block liquidations under load
Liquidation functions should be permissionless and gas-efficient so any bot can execute them under stress
A backstop/insurance fund is needed to absorb bad debt that occurs despite a well-tuned liquidation system

questions.title: Yield Vault Share Price Shows Compounding Rounding Drift
questions.prompt: An auto-compounding yield vault's share price (assets per share) shows tiny rounding discrepancies on individual deposits and withdrawals. Over several weeks of continuous activity, those small discrepancies have compounded into a real, measurable accounting drift between total vault assets and what the sum of all outstanding shares should be worth. Walk through your diagnosis and fix.
questions.modelAnswer: A drift that accumulates over many small transactions rather than appearing all at once points to integer-division rounding in the share price math being systematically biased in the wrong direction, rather than a one-time bug. On every mint and burn, the vault computes shares-for-assets or assets-for-shares using integer division, which truncates; the critical design question is which direction that truncation should favor. Correctly designed vaults always round in the protocol's (i.e., existing shareholders') favor: round down the shares minted for a deposit, and round down the assets returned for a withdrawal. If the implementation instead rounds in the user's favor on either operation — even by one wei per transaction — each individual action looks negligible, but across thousands of deposits and withdrawals over weeks, that consistent one-directional leak compounds into a real, measurable gap between the vault's actual asset balance and the theoretical value backing all outstanding shares. The diagnosis is to replay the transaction history and compute, for each mint/burn, which direction the rounding went relative to the 'correct' rounding convention; a systematic bias in one direction (rather than roughly balanced randomness) confirms the root cause. The fix is to use a rounding-aware math library (e.g., OpenZeppelin's `Math.mulDiv` with an explicit rounding mode) and audit every conversion point in the vault to ensure both directions always round against the user, never in their favor. I'd also add invariant tests asserting that total vault assets can never fall below the sum of all shares' claimable value at any point, which would have caught this before it reached production.
questions.professionalAnswer: The fact that this shows up as a slow compounding drift instead of one big obvious bug tells me it's not a logic error so much as a rounding bias baked into the share math that's been bleeding value in one direction the whole time. Every mint and burn in a vault like this involves integer division somewhere — converting assets to shares or shares back to assets — and division in Solidity truncates, so the real question is always which way that truncation is supposed to go. The correct convention is that rounding should always favor the vault, meaning existing shareholders, not whoever's doing the current transaction — round down the shares you mint on a deposit, round down the assets you pay out on a withdrawal. If even one of those two directions got it backwards, each individual transaction only leaks a tiny, invisible amount, but run that through thousands of deposits and withdrawals over a few weeks and it adds up to a real, measurable hole between what the vault actually holds and what all the outstanding shares are supposed to be worth. To confirm that's what's happening, I'd replay the transaction history and check, transaction by transaction, which direction the rounding actually went relative to what it should have been — if it's consistently one direction rather than random noise, that's the proof. The fix is to go through every conversion point in the vault and make sure it's using a rounding-aware math library, rounding against the user both ways, not just on the direction someone happened to think about first. And I'd want invariant tests in place going forward that specifically assert total vault assets never drop below what all the shares together are owed — that's exactly the kind of property-based check that would have caught this before it ever reached mainnet.
questions.example: A trace of 50 consecutive withdrawals shows the vault paying out 1 wei more than the mathematically exact amount in 47 of them (rounding up on withdrawal instead of down) — individually invisible, but summing to a measurable multi-token drift after several weeks of continuous activity.
commonMistakes: Treating each individual rounding discrepancy as negligible without checking for a systematic directional bias across many transactions
Rounding in the user's favor (even by one unit) on either minting or burning instead of always rounding against the user
Not auditing every single conversion point in the vault for consistent rounding direction
Using plain integer division without an explicit, intentional rounding mode
No invariant test asserting total assets can never fall below the value owed to all outstanding shares
keyPoints: A compounding drift (vs. a one-time bug) points to systematic rounding bias, not an isolated logic error
Correct vault design always rounds against the user: down on shares minted, down on assets paid out on withdrawal
Replaying transaction history to check rounding direction confirms whether bias is systematic
The fix requires auditing every conversion point for consistent rounding direction using a proper math library
Invariant tests asserting assets always cover shares' claimable value would catch this class of bug pre-production

questions.title: A Governance Proposal Passes After a Flash-Loaned Voting-Power Spike
questions.prompt: A governance proposal narrowly passed. On-chain analysis afterward shows an address flash-borrowed a large amount of the governance token immediately before the voting-power snapshot, voted, and returned the tokens immediately after — never holding them outside of that single transaction. Walk through your diagnosis of why this was possible and how you'd fix it.
questions.modelAnswer: This attack is only possible if the governance contract measures voting power from a balance that can be manipulated within the voting transaction itself, rather than from a snapshot taken before the proposal existed. The specific failure here is almost certainly that voting power was read via a live `balanceOf()` call (or an equivalent current-balance check) at the moment of voting, rather than via a checkpointed, block-number-indexed snapshot like the ERC20Votes/Compound-style `getPastVotes()` pattern. Because the attacker could flash-borrow tokens, vote, and return them all within one transaction, a live balance check sees the inflated balance at exactly the right moment and never has the opportunity to see the true, un-manipulated balance. Confirming this means checking whether the governance contract calls a checkpoint-based function tied to a specific historical block (ideally the proposal's creation or snapshot block, not the current block) versus a current-state balance check, and then confirming the attacker's transaction trace shows the classic borrow-vote-repay pattern atomically. The structural fix is to adopt checkpointed voting power: voting weight for any proposal must be read from the voter's balance as of a block strictly before the proposal was created, so tokens acquired after that point (including via flash loan) simply don't count no matter when within the voting window someone votes. For the proposal that already passed illegitimately, the response is procedural: if the governance system has an emergency veto/guardian mechanism or a timelock delay before execution, that window should be used to halt or cancel the proposal before its effects are enacted, and the team should communicate transparently about the incident and any parameter change needed to prevent recurrence.
questions.professionalAnswer: For this to work at all, the governance contract has to be checking voting power from something that can move within a single transaction, and reading it live at vote time rather than from a snapshot taken before the proposal existed is exactly that gap. My guess, and what I'd go verify first, is that the contract's voting function is calling something like a plain current `balanceOf()` instead of a proper checkpointed lookup — the ERC20Votes/Compound-style `getPastVotes()` pattern that ties voting weight to a specific historical block number. If it's reading live balance, then flash-borrow, vote, repay in one transaction works perfectly, because the live balance really is inflated at exactly the moment it's checked — there's no window where the contract would ever see the real, un-manipulated number. To confirm, I'd check the governance code for which function it calls to get voting weight, and separately pull the attacker's transaction trace to confirm the borrow-vote-repay pattern happened atomically, which it almost certainly did. The actual fix is to lock voting weight to a snapshot taken strictly before the proposal was even created — so it doesn't matter if you flash-borrow a mountain of tokens the second voting opens, those tokens didn't exist in your balance as of the snapshot block, so they just don't count, full stop, regardless of when during the voting window you cast your vote. As for the proposal that already passed this way — if there's a timelock or a guardian veto before it actually executes, that's the moment to use it, halt or cancel the thing before its effects land, and then be upfront with the community about exactly what happened and what's being changed in the voting mechanism so it can't happen the same way twice.
questions.example: Transaction trace shows: flash-borrow 2,000,000 GOV tokens → call `castVote()` on proposal #41 using current balance (inflating voting power past the quorum-tipping threshold) → repay the flash loan, all within one transaction at block 19,204,117 — one block before the snapshot height the contract should have used.
commonMistakes: Assuming the vulnerability is in the token or the flash loan mechanism rather than in how the governance contract measures voting power
Reading voting power from a live/current balance check instead of a checkpointed historical snapshot
Using a snapshot block that is too close to or after proposal creation, still leaving a manipulation window
Not having an emergency veto, guardian, or timelock mechanism to intervene before a maliciously-passed proposal executes
Treating the fix as purely technical without addressing the already-compromised proposal procedurally
keyPoints: The attack requires voting power to be readable from a balance that can change within a single transaction
Checkpointed voting power (ERC20Votes/getPastVotes-style), snapshotted before proposal creation, prevents this entirely
Confirming the exploit requires checking both the governance code's voting-power source and the attacker's transaction trace
Tokens acquired after the snapshot block (including via flash loan) must not count regardless of vote timing
A timelock/guardian veto is the needed procedural safety net for a proposal that already passed illegitimately

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly identifies live/current balance checking (vs. checkpointed snapshot) as the root cause
Explains why a snapshot must be taken before proposal creation to be effective
