Finally, the model should be paired with a reserve factor that diverts a percentage of interest paid by borrowers into a protocol-owned reserve, providing a buffer against bad debt and smoothing the system's resilience independent of the rate curve itself — the rate curve manages the liquidity/utilization dynamic, while the reserve factor manages solvency risk, and conflating the two into one mechanism would leave one of the two risks unaddressed.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd go with a kinked utilization curve, which is basically the industry-standard shape at this point, because the kink is specifically what resolves the push and pull here. Utilization is just total borrowed over total deposited. Below some target point — call it 80-90%, and I'd tune that per asset — I'd keep the borrow rate rising gently and linearly with utilization, because the goal below that point is to make borrowing cheap enough that capital actually gets put to work instead of sitting idle earning depositors nothing; idle, unborrowed capital is a real cost even though it feels 'safe.' But once utilization crosses that kink, I'd make the slope much steeper — rates should start climbing fast as utilization approaches 100%, because that's the zone where depositors are at real risk of not being able to withdraw, since their funds are literally out on loan. That steep climb does two things at once: it makes it expensive for borrowers to keep borrowing, pushing them to repay, and it makes supplying capital really attractive for new depositors chasing that yield, so you get pressure from both directions pulling utilization back down before you actually hit the wall. The depositor rate isn't something I'd set independently — I'd derive it directly from the borrow rate times utilization, minus whatever cut I'm taking as a reserve factor, so depositors automatically get paid more exactly when utilization is high and risk is elevated, which is the right incentive alignment. I wouldn't use one curve for every asset either — a volatile or thin-liquidity asset needs a lower kink and a much steeper post-kink slope than something like a major stablecoin, because a liquidity crunch is a lot more dangerous for the volatile asset. And I'd keep the reserve factor as a genuinely separate lever from the rate curve — the curve's job is managing the utilization/liquidity dynamic, the reserve factor's job is building a solvency buffer against bad debt, and I wouldn't try to make one mechanism do both jobs, because that's how you end up under-protected against whichever risk you didn't explicitly design for.
questions.example: At 70% utilization (below an 85% kink), the borrow rate might sit at 4% APR; if utilization spikes to 95% during a demand surge, the post-kink slope pushes the borrow rate to 40%+ APR, rapidly incentivizing repayments and new deposits that pull utilization back toward the target band.
commonMistakes: Using a single linear rate curve with no kink, failing to create urgency as utilization approaches full liquidity exhaustion
Setting the same kink and slope for all assets regardless of volatility or liquidity profile
Deriving the supply rate independently from the borrow rate instead of linking them through utilization, breaking the incentive alignment
Conflating the interest rate curve (liquidity/utilization management) with the reserve factor (solvency/bad-debt buffer) as if one mechanism handles both risks
Setting the kink too high for a volatile or illiquid asset, leaving too little room to react before a liquidity crunch
keyPoints: Kinked utilization-based rate curve: gentle slope below the kink to encourage lending, steep slope above it to protect depositor liquidity
Supply rate derived from borrow rate times utilization (minus reserve factor), aligning depositor incentive with rising risk
Per-asset tuning of kink position and post-kink slope based on volatility and liquidity profile
Reserve factor as a distinct solvency/bad-debt buffer, separate from the rate curve's liquidity-management role
The kink mechanism itself is what resolves the capital-efficiency vs. withdrawal-protection tension, not a single flat rate

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Proposes a kinked utilization-based rate curve and explains why the kink resolves the stated tension
Correctly derives the supply/depositor rate from the borrow rate and utilization
Discusses per-asset tuning of kink position/slope based on volatility and liquidity
Correctly separates the rate curve's liquidity role from the reserve factor's solvency role
Explains the incentive dynamics (borrower repayment pressure, depositor yield attraction) above the kink

questions.title: Modeling Initial Supply, Distribution, and Emission for a New Token
questions.prompt: Your protocol is launching a new governance/incentive token. Design a model for the token's initial total supply, how it's distributed across stakeholders (team, investors, treasury, community), and its emission curve over time, such that early incentives don't collapse the token's long-term value.
questions.modelAnswer: The modeling exercise has to start from the demand side, not the supply side: before fixing a total supply number, model the expected sources of ongoing token demand (governance participation requiring holding/locking, fee capture or buyback-and-burn mechanics, staking for a yield or utility benefit) because an emission schedule is only sustainable relative to demand it's being measured against — a supply schedule that looks reasonable in isolation can still crash price if demand growth is slower than token unlocks. For distribution, the standard allocation buckets (team/founders, investors, treasury/protocol-owned, community/ecosystem incentives) each need different vesting treatment calibrated to their incentive role: team and investor allocations should carry a cliff (commonly 12 months, during which zero tokens unlock) followed by linear vesting over 2-4 years, specifically to align those stakeholders with long-term protocol success rather than short-term price action, and to avoid a supply shock the moment of listing; treasury allocations should be governed by on-chain or multisig-controlled spending policy rather than released on a fixed timer, since treasury needs are use-case-driven, not time-driven; community/ecosystem incentive allocations (liquidity mining, airdrops) are the trickiest because they need to be released fast enough to bootstrap genuine usage but not so fast that the token becomes primarily a vehicle for farm-and-dump behavior — a decaying emission curve (high initial emissions tapering down, e.g., halving every N months or following a programmatic decay function) is the standard tool here, mirroring Bitcoin's halving logic in spirit: early high rewards compensate for high uncertainty/risk in being an early participant, while the taper prevents indefinite dilution. The emission curve and the vesting cliffs must be modeled together on a single unlock-schedule timeline, because the real risk isn't any single bucket's schedule in isolation but the sum of all unlocks landing in overlapping windows — a common real-world failure mode is a token whose team cliff ends in the same month as a large ecosystem-incentive unlock, creating a cumulative sell-pressure spike that the demand side (governance/staking/fee capture) hasn't grown enough to absorb. The model's output should be a chart of cumulative unlocked supply vs. projected demand-driven token velocity over time, stress-tested against a pessimistic demand-growth scenario, not just the optimistic base case.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd actually start on the demand side before even touching a total supply number, because an emission schedule only means anything relative to the demand it's competing against — if I design a 'reasonable-looking' unlock schedule without first modeling what's actually going to create ongoing demand for the token, whether that's governance locking, fee buybacks, or staking utility, I've designed in a vacuum. Once I've got a rough sense of expected demand growth, I'd split distribution into the usual buckets — team, investors, treasury, community — but treat each one's vesting very differently based on what incentive I'm actually trying to create. Team and investors get a real cliff, a year with nothing unlocking, then linear vesting over a few years after that, because the whole point is making sure those people are incentivized by the protocol's long-run health, not by dumping on day one. Treasury I wouldn't put on a fixed timer at all — I'd want that gated by actual governance or multisig spending decisions, because treasury spend should be driven by what the protocol needs to do, not by a calendar. Community incentives are the hard one — I need those to unlock fast enough to actually bootstrap real usage, but if I make them too generous too early, I just end up paying mercenary farmers who dump the second rewards taper, with no real users left behind. So I'd use a decaying emission curve there, high rewards early that step down over time — same logic as Bitcoin's halving, really — early high rewards compensate people for taking on more risk as early participants, and the taper stops it from diluting forever. But here's the part I think actually matters most and gets missed: I wouldn't model any of these buckets' schedules in isolation. I'd put every unlock — team cliffs, investor vesting, community emission decay — on one timeline and look for where they stack up, because the real danger isn't any one bucket dumping, it's two or three unlock events landing in the same window, creating a sell-pressure spike that whatever demand I've built up hasn't grown enough to absorb yet. And I'd stress-test that combined timeline against a pessimistic demand scenario, not just my optimistic base case, before I'd sign off on the model.
questions.example: If the team's 12-month cliff ends in month 13 at the same time a large liquidity-mining program's emissions peak, the model should flag that overlapping unlock spike as a risk, even if each schedule looked fine when reviewed independently, and suggest staggering one of the two.
commonMistakes: Designing the emission/unlock schedule before modeling expected token demand drivers, so supply and demand are never actually compared
Giving team and investor allocations no cliff or a very short one, creating immediate sell pressure at or shortly after listing
Releasing community/ecosystem incentives on a flat, non-decaying schedule that attracts only short-term farm-and-dump participation
Modeling each stakeholder bucket's vesting schedule in isolation instead of on one combined unlock timeline
Only stress-testing the optimistic demand-growth scenario instead of a pessimistic one against the combined unlock schedule
keyPoints: Model demand drivers (governance, fee capture, staking utility) before finalizing the supply/emission schedule
Cliff-plus-linear vesting for team/investor allocations to align incentives with long-term success
Governance- or policy-driven (not timer-driven) release for treasury allocations
Decaying emission curve for community/ecosystem incentives to bootstrap usage without encouraging farm-and-dump behavior
Combined unlock-schedule timeline across all buckets, stress-tested against pessimistic demand growth to catch overlapping unlock spikes

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Grounds the supply/emission design in modeled demand drivers rather than designing supply in isolation
Proposes appropriate vesting treatment (cliff + linear) for team/investor allocations
Proposes a decaying emission curve for community incentives with reasoning about farm-and-dump risk
Treats treasury allocation as governance/policy-driven rather than timer-driven
Models all unlocks on one combined timeline and stress-tests against overlapping unlock spikes/pessimistic demand

questions.title: Single Token vs. Split Utility/Governance Token Design
questions.prompt: Your protocol needs a token design decision: should it launch a single token that serves both as the governance token and as the in-protocol utility/fee token, or should it split those roles into two separate tokens? Walk through the tradeoffs of each approach.
questions.modelAnswer: A single combined token is the simpler, more common design and it has a real structural advantage: it concentrates all demand drivers (needing the token to pay fees, needing it to participate in governance, often needing it to stake for yield) onto one asset, which means usage growth directly feeds governance-token demand and vice versa, creating a flywheel where protocol success and governance-token value are tightly coupled — this alignment is valuable because it means the people with the most influence over protocol decisions (large token holders) are economically exposed to the consequences of those decisions in the same breath as users who just need utility. The downside is that combining the two roles forces every utility user to also be exposed to governance-token volatility and governance-driven value swings even if they have zero interest in governance, which can suppress utility adoption (a user who just wants to pay transaction fees shouldn't need to buy a volatile speculative asset to do so) and can also create governance capture risk, where entities that accumulate large utility-driven token positions (e.g., a market maker or heavy protocol user) end up with outsized governance power despite having no particular interest in exercising it well. A split design — a stable or more utility-focused fee/usage token plus a separate governance token — decouples these concerns: utility can be denominated in something more predictable (even a stablecoin-pegged fee mechanism in some designs), and governance power accrues specifically to a token acquired for the purpose of governing, generally through explicit staking/locking (vote-escrow style), which tends to filter for longer-term-aligned holders since locking is a costlier, more deliberate signal than simply holding. The cost of splitting is added complexity — two tokens to design, distribute, maintain liquidity for, and explain to users, and a weaker direct flywheel between usage growth and governance-token demand, since the two are no longer the same asset. The right choice depends on protocol maturity and user base: early-stage protocols often benefit from a single token to concentrate scarce liquidity and simplify the mental model for a growing community, while more mature protocols with a large, varied utility user base (where forcing fee-payers into governance-token exposure becomes a real adoption friction) are more likely to benefit from splitting, often introducing the governance-specific token (or a vote-escrow wrapper on the existing token) as the protocol matures rather than launching split from day one.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd frame this as a tradeoff between simplicity-and-alignment on one side and separation-of-concerns on the other, and the right call really depends on where the protocol is in its life. A single combined token is simpler to launch and explain, and it has a genuine benefit beyond just convenience — because the same token is needed for fees, for governance, and often for staking, every bit of usage growth feeds demand for the governance token directly, so the people who end up with the most governance power are also the people most economically exposed to the protocol's outcomes. That alignment is real and valuable. But the cost is that I'm forcing every utility user — someone who just wants to pay a transaction fee — to hold exposure to a volatile, governance-driven asset whether they care about governance or not, and that's genuine adoption friction for a certain kind of user. It also opens a governance-capture angle I'd flag specifically: if a market maker or a heavy protocol user ends up accumulating a lot of the token just through their normal activity, they can end up with outsized voting power they never actually sought and might not exercise carefully. A split design fixes both of those — utility gets denominated in something more predictable, and governance power only accrues to people who deliberately acquire and usually lock a separate governance token, which, because locking is costly and deliberate, tends to filter in favor of longer-term-aligned holders rather than passive accumulators. What I'd be honest about is the cost of splitting: now I've got two tokens to design, distribute, keep liquid, and explain to a community, and I've weakened that nice flywheel where usage growth directly drives governance-token demand, because they're not the same asset anymore. So my actual recommendation leans on maturity — an early-stage protocol trying to bootstrap a community and concentrate thin liquidity is usually better off with one token, and splitting, or layering something like a vote-escrow mechanism on top of the existing token, is a move I'd make once the protocol's grown a large and varied utility user base where that single-token friction has become a real, measurable adoption problem rather than a theoretical one.
questions.example: A lending protocol where the same token is needed to pay fees and vote on risk parameters may see a heavy borrower accumulate large token holdings purely through fee payments, giving them outsized governance influence over risk parameters despite no strategic interest in protocol governance — a risk a split utility/governance design would avoid.
commonMistakes: Treating single-token and split-token as equally simple decisions without weighing protocol maturity and user base variety
Missing the governance capture risk where heavy utility users accumulate outsized voting power unintentionally in a combined-token design
Assuming a split design has no real cost, ignoring the added complexity of distributing and maintaining liquidity for two tokens
Not recognizing that vote-escrow/locking mechanisms are what actually filter for long-term-aligned governance participants in a split design
Failing to connect the single-token flywheel (usage growth feeding governance-token demand) as the main benefit worth weighing against the split
keyPoints: Single token concentrates demand and tightly couples usage growth with governance-token value (a real flywheel benefit)
Single token forces utility users into governance-token volatility exposure and risks governance capture by heavy utility users
Split design decouples utility (more predictable) from governance (accrues to deliberate, often locked/staked holders)
Splitting adds real complexity: two tokens to design, distribute, and maintain liquidity for, with a weaker usage-to-governance flywheel
Recommendation should depend on protocol maturity and user base variety, not be treated as a universal default

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly explains the alignment/flywheel benefit of a single combined token
Correctly identifies utility-adoption friction and governance capture risk in a combined token
Correctly explains how a split design decouples utility from governance and what it gains
Acknowledges the real complexity/liquidity cost of splitting into two tokens
Frames the recommendation around protocol maturity/user base rather than a one-size-fits-all answer

questions.title: End-to-End DAO Governance Flow for Treasury Decisions
questions.prompt: Design the full on-chain governance flow for a DAO that controls a protocol treasury: how proposals are created, how voting works, what happens between a successful vote and execution, and how the design protects against both governance attacks and legitimate emergency needs.
questions.modelAnswer: The flow has four stages, each with its own protective mechanism: proposal creation, voting, a timelock delay, and execution. Proposal creation should require a minimum token threshold to submit (a 'proposal threshold') so that submitting proposals isn't free and spam-proof voting attention from genuinely considered proposals, and proposals should be formatted as executable calldata (target contract, function signature, parameters) rather than free-text intentions, so that what gets voted on is literally what will execute — a common real failure is a proposal whose text says one thing but whose attached calldata does something else, which only a calldata-level vote closes. Voting uses the governance token (commonly with block-number-snapshotted voting power to prevent flash-loan vote manipulation — borrowing tokens for one block to vote and returning them, which snapshotting at proposal-creation block defeats since borrowed tokens weren't held at that snapshot) over a fixed voting period long enough for the community to actually review and react (commonly 3-7 days), with both a quorum requirement (minimum total participation, so a tiny minority can't pass changes when most holders are simply inactive) and an approval threshold (simple majority or supermajority depending on the proposal's risk — routine treasury allocations might need simple majority, while changes to the governance process itself or very large treasury movements should require a supermajority, since the barrier to changing the rules of the game should be higher than the barrier to a normal spending decision). Between a successful vote and execution sits a timelock — a mandatory delay (commonly 24-72 hours, longer for higher-impact proposals) during which the already-approved transaction is queued but not yet executable; this is the single most important security control in the whole flow because it creates a window for the community to notice and react to an approved-but-malicious or exploited proposal before funds actually move, including the ability for a security council or emergency mechanism to cancel a queued malicious transaction within that window. For emergency needs that can't wait for the full proposal-vote-timelock cycle (e.g., pausing a contract under active exploit), the design should carve out a separate, narrower emergency path — typically a smaller, elected or multisig security council with strictly limited powers (pause/freeze only, never treasury withdrawal) and its own transparency/reporting requirement after acting, rather than widening the main governance path's speed at the cost of its safety, since the same timelock that protects against malicious proposals would also block a legitimate emergency response if it were the only path available.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd break this into four stages and think about what each one is actually protecting against, because that's the only way to avoid the trap of optimizing one stage at the expense of another. Proposal creation first — I'd require a minimum token threshold just to submit a proposal, so it's not free to spam the governance process, and critically, I'd require the proposal to be actual executable calldata, not a text description of intent, because the number of governance incidents that come down to 'the text said X but the calldata did Y' is not small, and a vote only really means something if people are voting on the calldata itself. For voting, I'd snapshot voting power at the block the proposal was created, specifically to kill flash-loan governance attacks — if voting power were based on current balance, someone could borrow a huge pile of tokens for one block, vote, and return them, and snapshotting at proposal creation means tokens borrowed after that point simply don't count. I'd run the vote over several days, long enough for people to actually notice and react, and I'd require both quorum and an approval threshold — quorum so a handful of active voters can't pass something when most holders are just asleep, and I'd scale the approval bar with the proposal's risk, simple majority for routine treasury spends, supermajority for anything that changes the governance rules themselves or moves a large chunk of the treasury, because changing the rules of the game should be harder than making a normal decision under those rules. Then — and I think this is the single most important piece in the whole design — between a passed vote and actual execution, I'd put a mandatory timelock, a day or two, maybe longer for bigger proposals. That delay exists purely to give the community a window to notice if something passed that shouldn't have, whether it's a bug, an oversight, or an actual attack, and to be able to cancel the queued transaction before it executes. The tension I'd call out directly is that this same timelock, which is protecting you from malicious proposals, would also block you from reacting to a genuine emergency, like an active exploit that needs a pause right now. I wouldn't solve that by weakening the timelock — I'd build a separate, narrow emergency path instead, something like a small elected security council with multisig control that can only pause or freeze, never move treasury funds, and that has to publicly report whatever it did afterward, so the emergency speed doesn't come at the cost of the main governance process's safety.
questions.example: A proposal to move 500,000 tokens from treasury to a new strategy passes a 5-day vote with quorum met; it then sits in a 48-hour timelock queue, during which a community member notices the attached calldata actually sends funds to an unintended address, and the security council cancels the queued transaction before execution.
commonMistakes: Voting on a text description of a proposal's intent rather than on the actual executable calldata, allowing a mismatch between stated intent and real effect
Using current token balance for voting power instead of a snapshot at proposal creation, exposing the vote to flash-loan manipulation
Having no timelock between a passed vote and execution, removing the window to catch and cancel a malicious or buggy proposal
Using a single uniform approval threshold for both routine spending decisions and changes to the governance process itself
Building an emergency path with powers broad enough to move treasury funds, effectively creating a backdoor around the main governance process
keyPoints: Proposal threshold plus calldata-based (not text-based) proposals so votes are on the actual executable action
Snapshotted voting power at proposal creation to prevent flash-loan governance manipulation
Quorum and risk-scaled approval thresholds (simple majority vs. supermajority) across the voting period
Mandatory timelock between vote success and execution as the key window to detect and cancel malicious/buggy proposals
Narrow, strictly-limited emergency path (pause-only, never treasury movement) separate from the main governance flow

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Specifies calldata-based proposals and a proposal threshold to prevent intent/execution mismatches and spam
Correctly uses snapshotted voting power to prevent flash-loan governance attacks
Includes quorum and risk-scaled approval thresholds for voting
Identifies the timelock as the critical security window between vote success and execution, with cancellation capability
Designs a separate, strictly limited emergency path that doesn't weaken the main governance process's safety

questions.title: Yield Farming Incentives Without Attracting Only Mercenary Capital
questions.prompt: Design a yield farming incentive program for a new liquidity pool. The design must avoid attracting only short-term 'mercenary capital' that provides liquidity purely to farm rewards and exits the moment rewards decrease, leaving the pool thin.
questions.modelAnswer: The root cause of mercenary capital is that flat, no-strings-attached reward emissions make the reward itself the entire investment thesis — capital shows up purely because the yield is high and leaves the instant it's not the highest yield available anywhere, with zero cost to leaving. The design has to introduce real switching costs or differentiated payouts tied to commitment, not just raise or lower the headline APR. The most direct lever is time-locked or boosted rewards: instead of paying out LP rewards continuously and freely withdrawable, reward multipliers scale with how long LP tokens have been staked (e.g., a vote-escrow-style boost where locking LP tokens for longer durations — 3 months, 1 year, 4 years — grants a proportionally larger share of the reward pool), which directly filters for capital willing to commit rather than capital optimizing for instant liquidity. A second lever is paying rewards partly in a vesting or locked form rather than fully liquid tokens on every claim — e.g., rewards vest linearly over weeks/months after being earned, so an LP who exits early forfeits unvested reward value, which raises the real cost of a quick in-and-out farm cycle without affecting LPs who intend to stay. A third lever, often combined with the above, is directing a meaningfully higher reward multiplier to LPs who also hold/lock the protocol's own governance token alongside their LP position (a 'boosted' farming design), which filters for participants who have an actual stake in the protocol's long-term success rather than purely mercenary yield-chasers, since accumulating and locking governance tokens is a costlier, more deliberate signal than simply depositing liquidity. Underlying all of this, the emission schedule itself should decay over time (front-loaded but tapering, rather than flat-forever), because a permanently flat high APR is itself what signals 'this is a farm-and-dump reward, not a sustainable yield' to sophisticated capital — a visibly decaying schedule paired with real fee-revenue-driven yield growing to replace it over time tells the market the reward's purpose is bootstrapping, not permanent subsidy, which is a more honest and more sustainable signal than pretending the subsidized APR is the long-run expected return.
questions.professionalAnswer: The mercenary capital problem exists because, with a flat reward program, the reward is the entire thesis — capital shows up because the APR is high, and the moment something else pays slightly more, it leaves, because there's zero cost to leaving. So the fix, in my mind, isn't tweaking the APR number up or down, it's building in actual switching costs so leaving isn't free. The lever I'd reach for first is time-locking with boosted multipliers — something like a vote-escrow model where locking your LP position longer, a few months versus a year versus several years, gets you a proportionally bigger share of the rewards. That directly filters for capital that's willing to commit, because someone optimizing purely for liquidity and flexibility isn't going to lock for a year just to chase yield. The second lever I'd pair with that is vesting the rewards themselves rather than paying out fully liquid tokens on every claim — rewards vest over weeks or months after being earned, so if someone farms for three days and bails, they're walking away from a chunk of unvested value. That raises the real cost of a quick farm-and-dump cycle without touching anyone who was planning to stick around anyway. Third, I'd specifically boost rewards for LPs who are also holding or locking the protocol's own governance token alongside their liquidity position — that's a much stronger signal of actual alignment with the protocol than just depositing capital, because locking governance tokens is a deliberate, costly action, not a passive one. And underneath all three of those, I'd make sure the emission schedule itself decays over time instead of staying flat forever — a permanently flat high APR is honestly a red flag to anyone sophisticated, because it signals the reward isn't sustainable and is purely a farm-and-dump subsidy. A visibly tapering schedule, with real protocol fee revenue growing underneath it to take over as the subsidy fades, is a much more honest signal, and it's the kind of program that actually attracts capital planning to stay for the protocol, not just for this week's reward rate.
questions.example: An LP who locks their position for 12 months earns a 3x reward multiplier versus an unlocked position, and even the unlocked position's rewards vest linearly over 30 days — so an LP who deposits, farms for two days, and withdraws forfeits most of the unvested reward and never qualifies for the multiplier that would have made their yield competitive elsewhere.
commonMistakes: Relying solely on raising or lowering the headline APR to compete for liquidity instead of building in real switching costs
Paying out all rewards as fully liquid tokens with no lock-up or vesting, so there's zero cost to farming briefly and exiting
Using a flat, non-decaying emission schedule that signals an unsustainable permanent subsidy to sophisticated farmers
Not differentiating rewards for LPs who also hold/lock the protocol's governance token versus purely mercenary liquidity
Ignoring that the fix needs to filter for committed capital rather than simply trying to out-bid competing pools on yield
keyPoints: Time-locked/vote-escrow-style reward boosts that scale with commitment duration, filtering for capital willing to commit
Vesting rewards over time rather than paying fully liquid rewards instantly, raising the real cost of quick farm-and-exit cycles
Boosted rewards for LPs who also hold/lock governance tokens, rewarding genuine protocol alignment over pure yield-chasing
Decaying (not flat) emission schedule that signals a sustainable bootstrap purpose rather than a permanent subsidy
Recognizing that competing purely on APR magnitude cannot solve the mercenary capital problem — real switching costs are required

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Identifies that flat, no-commitment rewards are the root cause of mercenary capital
Proposes time-locked/boosted reward multipliers tied to commitment duration
Proposes vesting of earned rewards to raise the cost of quick exits
Proposes boosted rewards for governance-token-aligned LPs as a filter for genuine commitment
Includes a decaying emission schedule and explains why a flat-forever schedule signals unsustainability

questions.title: Layered Test Strategy for a Lending Protocol Pre-Audit
questions.prompt: Design a layered test strategy — unit, fuzz, invariant, and fork tests — for a DeFi lending protocol before it's submitted for external audit. Explain what distinct class of bug each layer is actually designed to catch, and why no single layer is sufficient on its own.
questions.modelAnswer: Each layer targets a different class of bug precisely because each tests a different dimension of 'what could go wrong,' and conflating them (e.g., assuming a thorough unit suite makes fuzzing redundant) leaves real gaps. Unit tests verify specific, known scenarios against expected outputs — given these exact inputs (a specific deposit amount, a specific collateral ratio), does the function return the specific expected result — which is essential for pinning down intended behavior and catching regressions, but unit tests only ever test the scenarios the developer thought to write, so they're structurally blind to edge cases the developer didn't anticipate. Fuzz testing addresses exactly that blind spot by throwing a large volume of randomized inputs at individual functions to find inputs that cause a revert, an overflow, or an assertion failure the developer didn't think to test for directly — for a lending protocol, fuzzing withdraw/borrow amount parameters across extreme ranges (zero, max uint, amounts just above/below a collateral threshold) catches boundary bugs that scenario-based unit tests miss by construction, but fuzzing still tests one function call at a time and doesn't verify that the system's properties hold across sequences of interleaved operations. Invariant testing closes that gap by running long random sequences of calls across multiple functions (deposit, borrow, repay, liquidate, in arbitrary order and by multiple simulated actors) and checking that protocol-level invariants still hold after every sequence — e.g., 'total protocol debt never exceeds total collateral value adjusted for liquidation thresholds,' or 'the sum of all users' tracked balances never exceeds the actual token balance held by the contract' — which is the layer that actually catches the multi-step, stateful bugs (like an accounting drift after a specific sequence of partial liquidations) that are invisible to both unit and fuzz tests individually, since those bugs only manifest from a particular history of interactions, not from any single call. Fork testing runs the actual deployed bytecode and state of real mainnet contracts (via a forked RPC snapshot) so the protocol's integration with real external dependencies — the actual Chainlink oracle, the actual Aave/Compound contracts if composing with them, real token contracts with their actual quirks (fee-on-transfer, non-standard decimals) — is tested against reality instead of a simplified local mock that might not reflect those contracts' actual behavior, catching integration bugs that only exist because of assumptions baked into mocks. No layer substitutes for another: unit tests confirm correctness for known cases, fuzzing confirms robustness against single-call edge cases, invariant testing confirms system-wide properties hold across arbitrary interaction histories, and fork testing confirms real-world integration correctness — a protocol that only does three of these four has a specific, identifiable class of bug it has structurally no way of catching before audit or production.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd think about this less as 'four types of tests' and more as 'four different blind spots, and each layer exists to cover one of them.' Unit tests are the baseline — specific input, specific expected output, and they're great for pinning down intended behavior and catching regressions, but they only ever cover the scenarios I personally thought to write, so by definition they can't catch the edge case I didn't think of. That's exactly the gap fuzz testing fills — throwing a huge volume of randomized inputs at individual functions to surface things like an overflow or an unexpected revert at some boundary value I never would have manually tested, say a withdraw amount that's one wei above a collateral threshold. But fuzzing is still testing one function call at a time, and a lot of the scariest lending protocol bugs aren't single-call bugs, they're the result of a specific sequence of calls over time — so that's where invariant testing earns its place: running long random sequences across deposit, borrow, repay, liquidate, in arbitrary order with multiple simulated users, and checking after every single step that core properties still hold, things like total debt never exceeding collateral value adjusted for liquidation thresholds, or the sum of tracked balances never exceeding the contract's actual token balance. That's genuinely the only layer that catches an accounting drift that only shows up after, say, three partial liquidations happen in a particular order — unit and fuzz tests individually have no way to see that. And then fork testing is solving a totally different problem again — it's not about finding bugs in my own logic, it's about making sure my assumptions about the outside world are actually true, by running against the real deployed bytecode of the actual Chainlink oracle, the actual tokens, any protocol I'm composing with, instead of a simplified mock that might quietly not reflect how that real contract actually behaves, like a fee-on-transfer token or non-standard decimals. I'd be explicit in a review that these four layers aren't redundant with each other — a protocol that's only done unit and fuzz testing, however thorough, still has zero coverage on multi-step state-dependent bugs and zero coverage on real-world integration quirks, and that's exactly the kind of gap an audit will not reliably catch for you either, so skipping a layer isn't a shortcut, it's a specific unaddressed risk category going into audit.
questions.example: An invariant test running randomized sequences of borrow/repay/liquidate calls surfaces a case where, after a specific sequence of partial liquidations, total tracked user debt sums to slightly more than the protocol's actual collateral backing — a drift that never appears in any single-call unit or fuzz test because it only emerges from that particular multi-step history.
commonMistakes: Treating a thorough unit test suite as sufficient coverage, missing edge cases the developer never thought to write a scenario for
Running fuzz tests only on isolated functions and assuming that also validates multi-step, stateful system properties
Skipping invariant testing, leaving no coverage for accounting drift or state corruption that only emerges from specific sequences of calls
Testing entirely against local mocks of external dependencies (oracles, composed protocols, tokens) instead of fork testing against real deployed contract behavior
Assuming audit will catch gaps left by a thin test suite instead of treating thorough layered testing as a prerequisite to a productive audit
keyPoints: Unit tests verify known scenarios but are structurally blind to unanticipated edge cases
Fuzz testing finds single-call boundary/edge-case bugs via randomized inputs that unit tests miss by construction
Invariant testing is the only layer that catches multi-step, stateful bugs by checking system-wide properties across arbitrary call sequences
Fork testing validates integration against real deployed external contracts (oracles, composed protocols, real tokens) instead of simplified mocks
Each layer covers a distinct, non-overlapping class of bug; omitting any one leaves a specific, identifiable gap going into audit

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly distinguishes unit tests' known-scenario coverage from their blindness to unanticipated edge cases
Correctly explains fuzz testing's role in catching single-call boundary bugs
Correctly explains invariant testing as the layer that catches multi-step, stateful/accounting bugs via system-wide properties
Correctly explains fork testing's role in validating real external-dependency integration over mocks
Clearly argues no single layer is sufficient, each covering a distinct non-overlapping bug class

questions.title: CI/CD Gate on Test Coverage and Static Analysis for a Contracts Repo
questions.prompt: Design a CI/CD pipeline for a smart contract repository that blocks every merge to main unless it meets test coverage thresholds and passes static analysis (Slither/Mythril) checks. Cover what the pipeline actually enforces, how findings are triaged, and how the gate avoids both false security and developer friction that leads to the gate being bypassed.
questions.modelAnswer: The pipeline needs distinct stages for distinct guarantees, run on every pull request, not just before release: a test stage running the full unit/fuzz/invariant suite with a coverage report generated per run, gated against a minimum line/branch coverage threshold (commonly 90%+ for core logic, calibrated per directory since peripheral/scripts code doesn't need the same bar as core accounting logic) so the gate measures something concrete rather than 'tests exist,' and a static analysis stage running Slither (fast, good signal-to-noise for common patterns) and optionally Mythril or a symbolic execution tool (slower, deeper, often run less frequently, e.g., nightly or pre-release rather than on every PR, to avoid making every PR wait on a slow analysis) against the changed contracts. The critical design decision is how findings are triaged, because static analyzers produce real false positives and the common failure mode is one of two extremes: either the team ignores findings entirely (false security, defeating the point of running the tool) or the team requires every finding resolved before merge (friction so high that developers start suppressing or disabling the check entirely, which is worse than not having it). The right middle path is a severity-tiered gate: high/critical severity findings (reentrancy, unchecked external calls, access control issues) block the merge outright and require either a code fix or an explicit, reviewed inline suppression comment justifying why the finding is a false positive in this specific context (which itself gets reviewed in the PR, so suppression isn't a silent escape hatch); medium/low findings are surfaced as PR comments requiring an explicit acknowledgment (a reviewer or author checkbox/comment) but don't hard-block merge, since blocking on every stylistic or low-confidence finding is exactly what drives teams to disable the whole check. Coverage thresholds should similarly be enforced on the diff (new/changed lines meeting a higher bar, e.g., 100% branch coverage on new logic) rather than only on the aggregate repo number, because an aggregate-only gate lets a well-tested legacy codebase mask a poorly-tested new feature merged on top of it. Finally, the pipeline's gate itself needs to be something that can't be silently bypassed — branch protection rules requiring the CI check to pass before merge, not just a visible-but-ignorable status, and the suppression-comment mechanism for high-severity findings should itself be auditable (tracked in version control, visible in review) so 'why was this allowed through' is always answerable later.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd split this into stages that each enforce something concrete, running on every PR, not just at release time. One stage runs the full test suite and spits out a coverage number, gated against a real threshold — I'd set that high for core accounting logic, 90%+, and lower it for scripts or peripheral code, because a single flat number across the whole repo either lets core logic skate by too easily or makes peripheral code annoyingly expensive to touch. Another stage runs static analysis — Slither for fast, decent-signal checks on every PR, and something heavier like Mythril running less often, nightly or pre-release, because it's slow enough that making every single PR wait on it is how you train developers to resent and eventually route around the gate. The part I'd actually spend the most design effort on is how findings get triaged, because I've seen this fail in both directions — either nobody looks at the findings and the whole check is security theater, or every single finding blocks merge and developers start disabling the linter in frustration, which is strictly worse than not running it at all. So I'd tier it by severity: anything high or critical — reentrancy, unchecked external calls, access control gaps — hard-blocks the merge, full stop, and the only way past it is either an actual fix or an explicit suppression comment in the code explaining why it's a false positive in this specific context, and that suppression itself has to go through code review, so it's not a silent escape hatch anyone can just add. Medium and low findings I'd surface as PR comments that need an acknowledgment, but I wouldn't hard-block on those, because blocking on every low-confidence or stylistic finding is exactly the friction that gets a whole gate turned off six months later. I'd also gate coverage on the diff, not just the aggregate repo number — new or changed lines should need a much higher bar, close to 100% branch coverage, because otherwise a well-tested old codebase can mask a brand-new, poorly-tested feature that just got merged on top of it. And none of this matters if the gate can be clicked past — I'd make sure branch protection actually requires the CI checks to pass, not just display a status, and I'd make sure every suppression comment lives in version control and goes through review, so if someone asks 'why did this finding get through' six months later, there's a real answer sitting in the PR history.
questions.example: A PR introduces a new withdrawal function with a Slither-flagged reentrancy warning; the pipeline blocks the merge until the developer either adds a reentrancy guard or provides a reviewed inline suppression comment explaining why the specific call pattern isn't exploitable, while a separate low-severity 'unused variable' finding on the same PR is surfaced as a comment without blocking.
commonMistakes: Gating only on aggregate repo-wide coverage, letting a poorly-tested new feature hide behind a well-tested legacy codebase
Hard-blocking merge on every static analysis finding regardless of severity, creating friction that leads teams to disable the check entirely
Allowing silent, unreviewed suppression of findings, turning the suppression mechanism into an unaudited bypass
Running slow, deep analysis tools (e.g., Mythril) on every PR instead of a faster subset, creating CI friction that drives workarounds
Relying on a visible-but-not-enforced CI status instead of actual branch protection requiring the check to pass before merge
keyPoints: Separate test-coverage and static-analysis stages, each enforcing a concrete, measurable threshold on every PR
Diff-based coverage gating (high bar on new/changed lines), not just aggregate repo-wide coverage
Severity-tiered finding triage: high/critical hard-blocks with reviewed suppression option, medium/low surfaced but non-blocking
Suppression of findings must be explicit, in-code, and go through review, never a silent bypass
Branch protection must actually enforce the CI gate (required status check) rather than a bypassable advisory status

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Designs concrete, separately-gated test-coverage and static-analysis CI stages
Gates coverage on the diff/new code, not only the aggregate repository number
Proposes a severity-tiered triage approach balancing false security against developer friction
Requires reviewed, auditable suppression rather than silent bypass of findings
Specifies enforced branch protection so the gate cannot be silently skipped
